title: Grazing sheep in fields with solar arrays
body_text: Sheep grazing in solar fields offers farmers economic, ecological gains | Cornell Chronicle Skip to main content Toggle navigation Search Cornell University Cornell.edu Media Relations Search Cornell University Cornell Chronicle Topics Architecture & Design Artificial Intelligence Arts & Humanities Business, Economics & Entrepreneurship Computing & Information Sciences Energy, Environment & Sustainability Food & Agriculture Global Reach Health, Nutrition & Medicine Law, Government & Public Policy Life Sciences & Veterinary Medicine Physical Sciences & Engineering Social & Behavioral Sciences Research Matters Campus & Community News & Events Local Impact NYS Impact New York City Public Engagement Features Photos of the Week Student Life Staff News Big Red Sports Inclusion and Belonging University Statements In Memory Around Cornell All Stories Podcast Media Relations Cornellians Credit: Sreang Hok/Cornell University A solar farm in Lansing, New York. Sheep grazing in solar fields offers farmers economic, ecological gains By Krisy Gashler College of Agriculture and Life Sciences October 14, 2026 Two new research papers shed light on the growing practice of grazing sheep in fields with solar arrays. One demonstrates that, in the right numbers, sheep grazing increases populations of beneficial insects like bees and lady beetles compared to mowing around solar panels. The other research describes a decision-making support tool to help farmers profitably grow their solar grazing herds. A team from the College of Agriculture and Life Sciences (CALS) found that when two sheep per hectare graze around solar arrays, the abundance of wild bees, honey bees and lady beetles jumped by 38%, compared to a control plot that was mowed. The increase was driven primarily by an 83% increase in honey bees alone, according to the team’s findings in “ Low solar-grazing densities support beneficial insects in agrivoltaic systems ,” published Oct. 7 in Environmental Research Letters. “Sheep grazing and beneficial insect habitat are two prominent conversation topics around solar development right now,” said Leana Zoller, the paper’s first author and a postdoctoral associate in natural resources in the Cornell CALS Ashley School of Global Development and the Environment. “But what’s been missing is research that treats them as parts of the same system. When we talk about sustainable solar development, integrating these discussions into a single framework is really helpful to farmers and community decision makers.” For three years, Zoller and a team of entomologists, ecologists and animal and plant scientists tested various stocking rates – how many sheep per hectare are allowed to graze a certain plot of land – using Cornell’s teaching sheep grazing at the university-owned  Cascadilla Community Solar Farm in Dryden, New York. At four sheep per hectare, they found beneficial insect abundance was similar to the mowed control site, while vegetation management effectiveness was greater than at two sheep per hectare. At eight sheep per hectare, vegetation management was maximized and sheep flock health remained high, but honey bee abundance dropped by 45%. “We zeroed in on stocking rates because that’s a concrete number that sheep farmers understand and work with every day, and we want this research to be useful,” said  Steve Grodsky , paper senior author and assistant professor of natural resources in the Ashley School. “With solar grazing, people, energy, agricultural animals, plants and insects are all part of this ecosystem. We’re trying to understand the connections between those pieces so that when solar developers, municipalities looking at solar development, or farmers are faced with a decision, they can have scientific information about potential trade-offs and synergies.” Grodsky is also assistant unit leader of the U.S. Geological Survey New York Cooperative Fish and Wildlife Research Unit. Additional co-authors are sheep farmer and solar grazing consultant Nikola Kochendoerfer, Ph.D. ’20;  Antonio DiTommaso , professor in the School of Integrative Plant Science; John Losey , professor of entomology;  Scott McArt , Ph.D. ’12, associate professor of entomology; Paige Muñiz, formerly a technician in McArt’s lab; and  Todd Ugine , Ph.D. ’04, research associate in Losey’s lab, all in CALS.  Sarah Carson , director of Cornell’s Campus Sustainability Office, was key in coordinating site access between researchers and the solar company that manages the Cascadilla solar farm. Another Cornell research team, from the Cornell SC Johnson College of Business, has developed a tool that helps farmers whose sheep graze in solar arrays to make better decisions about their operation. The team described the tool in “ Flock Management for Solar Grazing ,” which published Sept. 28 in Manufacturing & Service Operations Management. After a chance encounter with Caleb Scott, Ithaca-based sheep farmer and founder of  United Agrivoltaics ,  Vincent Slaugh , assistant professor at the Cornell Peter and Stephanie Nolan School of Hotel Administration and first author of the paper, began thinking through the economics and logistics of solar grazing. He recruited  Linwei Xin , associate professor of operations research and information engineering, and  Shane Henderson , Charles W. Lake, Jr. Professor in Productivity, both in the Cornell Duffield College of Engineering, to work on the topic. Together, they developed a spreadsheet-based model that helps sheep farmers to optimize procurement and sales decisions, based on factors like target flock size, costs, anticipated revenues, and expected vegetation in particular solar sites; if a farmer doesn’t have enough sheep to keep the grass down, they’ll have to cut it some other way. It also helps solar developers understand growers’ needs and develop contracts that are more profitable and sustainable for all parties long-term. United Agrivoltaics has already incorporated the tool into its onboarding process. Slaugh sees opportunity for U.S. shepherds to grow their operations – especially with solar contracts offering a steady source of income and animal feed. Current domestic sheep production for meat and wool doesn’t come close to meeting domestic demand; about  half of all lamb and mutton consumed in the U.S. is imported , primarily from New Zealand and Australia. “If we grow the sheep industry, will the American diet eventually include more lamb? Could that be a side effect of the solar energy revolution? I think the answer is very likely yes,” Slaugh said. “And then when that happens, we’d expect processors and supporting industries to come back, for banks to be willing to give more loans, and for supply chains to follow. All of that grows the economy, and rural economies in particular.” Kochendoerfer, who grazes 700 ewes on solar installations in New York and Vermont, said that economy is already growing.  “I work with a lot of farms that are now scaling up because of solar,” Kochendoerfer said. “There is a new wave of sheep farmers who are capitalizing on this access to good land. With solar grazing, you get paid to graze as opposed to having to pay to graze. That leads to sustainable, meaningful economic income that these farmers can use to expand, build a barn, buy equipment or hire someone. It’s enabling a lot of folks to build sound, viable agricultural businesses.” Funding for these research projects came from the Cornell Atkinson Center for Sustainability, the National Institute for Food and Agriculture and the National Science Foundation. Krisy Gashler is a writer for the College of Agriculture and Life Sciences. title: Frame – 31.5" color ePaper display
body_text: Introducing Frame | TRMNL About Blog Developers Integrations For Business Discover Login Sign up About Blog Developers Integrations For Business Discover Case Studies Login Sign up ← Back to all posts Introducing Frame November 16, 2026 image-lightbox#open keydown.enter->image-lightbox#open turbo:before-cache@document->image-lightbox#close"> tl;dr our 3rd release, a full color 31.5" ePaper display in a handmade wooden frame, is now available for pre-order. watch the short film: the 1st batch is just ~470 units and i intend to ship at least a few by the end of 2026. most deliveries will happen early 2027. see logistics for more details or pre-order here . background in 2013 i founded ArtSpot. our vision was to give New Yorkers a bit of joy by exposing them to local art. we did this through informal agreements with dozens of cafes, small galleries, and restaurants. " let us curate art on your walls, get paid if someone buys it. " and it worked. sort of. finding artists was easy, building the platform was easy. getting permission from venues was slow but straightforward. the problem was nobody actually bought the art. i remember the admin email notification that first time a piece was sold. it was a small painting of Janelle Monáe. the buyer was my friend, a gift to me. here it is, still in my possession. anyway ArtSpot failed. five years later i paid back my investors (+ 13% interest). but the vision never went away. i love making and consuming art. opinionated platform i probably say " the most popular feature request since launch is ______ " too often. after saying no (and yes) to so many requests, it's tough to keep count. but with certainty, one of our strongest convictions was about color. TRMNL is not a television. it is not a clock. we avoid trying to do too much. then grayscale happened . photos look great. art is possible. community member Clark debuted Jaws (yes the movie), 1 frame at a time . 1-bit Jaws on TRMNL which got us thinking... maybe we were wrong about color. maybe it aligns with our vision and just maybe, it makes it even bigger. introducing Frame today i'm thrilled to bury the lede and announce Frame . it's a 31.5 inch full color ePaper display, enclosed in a hand made wooden body that we manufacture ourselves. yes, we opened our own woodworking shop a few miles from HQ. a closer look at the workshop is coming soon. Schedule + Weather + Art in 1 screen Frame gets all the same features as other TRMNL devices, with a few additional perks spanning both the web platform and the hardware itself. watch the short film or read along below. Clock Sync often requested, always ignored, until now. Frame will update at specified moments of the day versus a relative "every N minutes" cadence. this reduces screen flicker while also extending the battery life and adding continuity to your schedule. Offline Mode the best interface is no interface the internet is cool but totally unnecessary. Frame's microSD port lets you run devices completely offline with zero personal information reaching our servers. Dedicated Power (optional) 1st port is available on the side panel like all TRMNL devices, a rechargeable battery is included (10-20k mAh available). but with Frame we added an extra USB-C port on the rear of the device, accessible with a small hole through the back panel for always-on connectivity. Color Expertise Lazarus workbench some of my colleagues are snobs about ePaper dithering algorithms and LUTs (look-up tables). this is now your gain. over the past few months we've been developing Lazarus, a color conversion engine that we think provides Frame the best color matching on the market for any Spectra 6 display. it's also coming soon to our 4-color device , and yes it will be open source for your own tuning pleasure. Three Orientations Frame at Cafe Brûlée in LaGrange, Georgia Hang Frame in portrait or landscape orientation without additional hardware, both are built-in and flush mounted. You can optionally buy or build your own kickstand. And More we're negotiating with some of our favorite community developers to build more Frame-centric features. paying homage to ArtSpot , we just created a Local Art plugin where anyone can submit their work and even sell it through the TRMNL platform. transparent supply chain before TRMNL i spent 10 years in b2b software and knew nothing about making physical products for everyday people. nobody ever blasted me on reddit about injection mold flow lines or damaged UPS packages. at best i'd get a G2 review every 3 months. this all changed in July 2024 and after shipping 60,000 devices to 79 countries we've gotten pickier about operational design. chief among these new requirements is doing as much production as possible in-house. here are Frame's components and where they're sourced: Component Location Lead Times Inventory EPD (31.5" screen) Overseas 2-3 months 300 in warehouse, 200 en route Packaging Alabama, USA 1-2 months samples received, design tweaks sent for larger batch Wooden body TRMNL shop, Pine Mountain, Georgia 1 week made-to-order pending wood species chosen at checkout USB-C Charging Cable and Block Overseas 3-4 weeks 500 in warehouse, includes American + European style adapters Plastic parts TRMNL HQ, LaGrange, Georgia 1-2 days made daily from a growing fleet of 3D printers PCBA Overseas 2-3 weeks 1,000 full assemblies (raw components) in warehouse, bulk pick & place order TBD Fasteners Overseas + USA 2-3 weeks 500 full assemblies ordered, en route next week Rigid foam Overseas + USA 1 week 50 in warehouse, 450 en route Batteries Overseas 2-3 weeks Samples in warehouse, 800 ordered, en route next week by reducing complexity, learning from past releases, and having everything we need either in stock or on order, i expect this to be our smoothest fulfillment cycle yet. as with other devices, all Frames are assembled by our own team and never outsourced. logistics Batch #1 is available to customers in locations our USA warehouse already ships to: USA, Canada, Mexico, Australia. pre-order here . we're open to shipping elsewhere, but Duty / Import fees could be quite high given the product's Customs value. to participate in Batch #1 as a resident outside these countries , go here . this option may be de-activated without notice if inventory sells out. in early 2027 we plan to open a 2nd woodworking shop near our Berlin, Rust changed me as a developer
body_text: Secret Weblog • How Rust Changed Me As A Developer 🫥 '> Secret Weblog blog archive tags How Rust Changed Me As A Developer By Martijn Faassen  •  2026-11-16  •  Tags:  programming ,  rust How Rust Changed Me As A Developer The programming language you use affects how you think as a software developer 1 . That may seem surprising to you; you may have picked up JavaScript pretty quickly knowing Python, and it didn't really affect how you think or develop. That's because those languages are pretty similar. The more different a programming language is from what you're used to, the more it can change you. Rust was quite different to me, so it did. I've been developing with Rust for over 6 years; more than 4 years professionally now . One of the reasons I really wanted to become more proficient with Rust is because I knew it would challenge me, and hopefully change me for the better as a developer. I think it did. What I learned and am going to discuss here is not exclusive to Rust. You can encounter many of these concepts in other contexts, and indeed I had encountered quite a few of them already. But in this case, Rust helped bring them into better focus. Where were enums all my life? We're all familiar with product types, though not usually under that name: struct Human { first_name : String, last_name : String, } The fields of the Human struct 2 can vary independently from each other, and we have to deal with all possible combinations: all possible first names and last names, combined. The product of their combinations, to to speak. But it turns out there's another type thing that's been around forever but that the programming community has mostly been been ignoring 3 : the sum type. A sum type expresses variants: something is either one thing, or another, out of a bunch of variants: enum Person { Human { first_name: String , last_name: String }, Cat { name: String , cuteness: Cuteness } } A Person is either a human or a cat: that's the sum of the possiblities. Each variant can have data associated with it, and this can be a product type, but the Person type is just these options (two in this case). In code where you need to deal with a person, you need to handle each variant by match in on the object. The Rust compiler enforces this. match some_person { Human { first_name, last_name } => { // do a thing with first_name and last_name }, Cat { name, cuteness } => { // do a thing with name and cutenes } } When you handle the human variant, you only need to worry about first_name and last_name . You don't have to worry about name or cuteness at all. These cases are distinct from each other. It turns out that it's really helpful to model stuff using sum types. People using functional programming languages already knew this. You can model optionality ( null ) this way: you got either some value, or nothing. You can also model errors: it's either okay (with whatever value you return in case of success), or an error (with a value describing the error). Any language without sum types now feels impoverished to me. I know I can simulate it with some type field, but the job of a programming language is to help me handle basic stuff, and this is basic stuff. Enums and abstraction In an object oriented programming language, you handle variants using dynamic dispatch and an interface (or inheritance). You do this: interface Person { def do_one_thing() def do_another_thing } class Human implements Person { ... } class Cat implements Person { ... } The idea is that you can now use Person anywhere without worrying about the details inside: it's loosely coupled. You only use their interface. This is indeed a great idea, but Rust taught me that this has tradeoffs I may not want to pay for. You pay two things: performance, and the need to create the interface. Let's talk about the need to create the interface. You need to devise an interface that actually makes sense for your application: how are you using humans and cats everywhere? Doing this work of abstraction may be extremely worthwhile to do, especially if you anticipate unknown future persons that you need to be able to plug in later without having to modify the code that uses them -- you want your code use the open/closed principle . But what if you are developing a single domain, and inside that you just want to be able to handle cats and humans and that's it? There's just no need to plug in other types of persons, and certainly not from outside. Or let's say you do want to add a new variant once every while. Say you want to add Dog . Maybe you're actually okay going through the code that handles Human and Cat and add handling for dogs too? Maybe it actually is helpful to see those other handlers right there too when you do so? The compiler is going to ensure you don't miss any spots! Or what if the abstraction you are trying to devise is the variance and that's more or less what you can say about it? For error handling, the abstraction is either okay with some value, or some error value. In this case you may be paying the price of creating an interface without it being worthwhile. enum may be all you actually need -- low ceremony, and statically checked. Finally I'll note that enums don't lock you out from creating that abstraction - you can add methods to an enum too, just like on a struct. Enums made me a better programmer as now I have another elementary, simple, easy to understand language construct for abstraction in my mental toolbox. Dispatch galore In many languages there are two types of dispatch: dynamic dispatch, which we've discussed in case of our Person interface, and conditional dispatch, like this: if something { do_this_thing() } else do_another() } Rust has dynamic dispatch, if you ask for it. It also has the powered up version of conditional dispatch I already discussed: match on enums. It has conditional dispatch too - that's just [a special case][https://docs.rs/bool/latest/bool/enum.Boolean.html]. There's another type of dispatch that Rust makes you think about: dispatch that's statically compiled. What if you're dealing either with groups of humans or groups of cats, and you want to do some operations on them, and those operations have common behavior (say, you want to count them). The group, or collection, doesn't really care about what's in it, as long as every item fulfills certain basic properties. You could create an enum Person ; either an enum or an interface with multiple implementations, and then dispatch during runtime to every member of the group based on whether that entry is a human or a cat. But this means you have to account for mixed groups of humans and cats, even though we just said those don't actually exist. Instead, you can express this differently in Rust. You still have a Person interface (trait), but you compose your individual type of Person ( Human or Cat ) during compile time. struct Group <T> { // some fields } // compile time assembly, // then runtime creation of the assembled group of cats let cat_group: Group<Cat> = Group::new(); Rust now refuses to compile if you use non-cat operations on items in the group, That's an invariant you now do not need to worry about anymore. This will be familiar to you with generics in other languages like TypeScript or Python. In Rust, when you process your group of cats, there is no individual check somewhere whether an entry is a human or a cat, as it already knows it's all cats before the program even ran. Rust directly dispatches to the cat code, and the human code is not play. You avoid indirect dispatch for every group member, which can matter in situations where performance is important. Rust made me a better programmer as I now better understand the connection between dispatch and performance. Type driven development When I discovered Python coming from C++ back in the late 1990s, dynamic typing was a revelation. You could so much with so little ceremony. For the last decade or so I have been on a long winding road back to types (far more ergonomic types) and more ceremony. I have the impression many have been on this journey along with me 4 . Types can statically check your code before it runs. In Rust, they can help the compiler compile stuff down to really high performance code. Both are great. But types can also have more subtle benefits. Let me get into this by analogy. Why create automated tests? Obvious : Automated tests ensure various properties of your code work and remain working. Subtle : Writing tests forces you to think about the architecture and APIs you're implementing more carefully. Making code testable can lead to better architecture. This is the insight of test driven development. Why write documentation? Obvious : People (and now machines) can understand 5 the why and what of your software by reading the documentation. Subtle : The act of writing the documentation can force you think about the architecture and APIs of your software. If you can't write about it, maybe you haven't gotten it right yet? That's documentation driven development. Why write types? Obvious : Statically check your code before it runs! Prevent runtime errors! Performance! Subtle : You model the domain model using types, trying to make sure it hangs together. Enums are really valuable here. You express parse, don't validate in them. The types guide the architecture and APIs of your software. This perhaps sounds like big design up front processes where people write all the tests, or all the docs, or all the types, in advance, and then do the implementation. 6 I'm not talking about this -- I'm talking about iterative development where you keep going back to tests, docs and types as you learn. Rust brought into focus how types are yet another tool to help me think while I develop. Rust made me a better programmer as it let me fully embrace type driven development. The Biggest Surprise Here is the biggest surprise I had coming to Rust. Much of the behavior I associated with dynamic interpreted languages with a rich runtime like Python can actually be done statically in Rust using macros. Let's talk about magic. Say you want to dump the state of a Python object -- you inspect all its fields, look at their type, turn each into a string, combine all the strings together into a big one. Now you can store it somewhere. Later on you restore that string back into an object. You can save and load any objects: magic! Python calls this pickle . What if you need to serialize to JSON? Python has a type system, and a library like Pydantic inspects the type objects during runtime and then uses this information to let you automatically serialize a Python object to JSON, or parse it back into Python again. More magic! Rust is a compiled language. Types aren't runtime objects. Without reflection, which takes special effort , runtime introspection of types is not a thing in Rust. But Rust can still do what Pickle and Pydantic do, at compile time. With serde , Rust's answer to pickle and Pydantic, you use a normal Rust type, annotate it with a few declarations, and then you can serialize it to JSON, or toml config format, and many other formats, and load it back again. The annotation looks like this: #[ derive (Serialize, Deserialize)] struct Human { first_name : String, last_name : String } With clap , you create the type that expresses exactly what command line arguments you expect (with enum s too!), document it using the normal way you document any API in Rust, and boom, you have a CLI with built in help. The code that handles the various cases gets well-typed data - at that point it's been parsed correctly already, using the same type you used to express the CLI. Like this: /// My first CLI #[ derive (Parser)] struct MyFirstCli { /// How many cats do you want? #[ arg (long, short)] amount_of_cats : usize } Again declarative #[] stuff going on. It looks a lot like decorators in Python. But Python decorators are executed during runtime, and we just said Rust doesn't normally let you do that. How does that work in Rust? Macros! Macros lets you write code that generates code during compile time. With serde, the macro generates a whole bunch of serialization code and deserialization code for the types annotated with it. This generated code gets compiled along with the rest of your code. The compiler can optimize it just like any other code. Code generation is scary. Macros are scary. Doing introspection in a dynamically typed language is a lot easier than using Rust macros, where code is parsed and generated. Macros shouldn't be randomly mixed with application code; macros belong in frameworks. That said, something being easy doesn't mean it should be used casually: in Python you typically want to carefully encapsulate your magic in a declarative framework too. Rust made me a better programmer as I learned about a new class of framework patterns. Ownership and Architecture Rust famously lets you write code without memory leaks that doesn't use a garbage collector. It also stops you from mutating data you're also reading elsewhere, making it impossible to stumble into whole classes of weird undefined behavior, especially with code that runs in parallel. Rust's ownership system is one of the main things that makes learning Rust hard. Python, JavaScript, Java and many other languages have mutable references everywhere, and you can just create cyclic data structures. Rust won't let you do either out of the box. The equivalent of this does not compile in Rust: class Item : def __init__ ( self , value ): self .value = value class Container : def __init__ ( self , items ): self .items = items my_item = Item() my_container = Container() my_container.items.append(my_item) my_item.value = "I change you!" This also doesn't compile: class Node : def __init__ ( self , parent , value ): self .parent = parent self .value = value self .children = [] def add_child ( self , node ): node.parent = self self.children.append(node) Rust won't just let you have circular references, in this case both children and a parent reference. This feels very limiting at first! What do you do instead? For mutating stuff, you learn how to separate mutation (often during construction) from using your data. That is a thing that's good to do in many contexts -- less invariants makes it's easier to reason about, but it takes a bit of getting used to Rust strictly enforcing it. For circular references it's trickier. I will go into it next, when I discuss arenas. A weird thing happens: if you lean into this friction it can improve the architecture of your codebase. Code becomes less coupled. It's hard to create weird backchannels with action at a distance that makes code difficult to understand, test and debug 7 . Rust code locally can be difficult to understand. But how the data flows, what does what, in the larger codebase, tends to be cleaner. Rust made me a better programmer as I now think about ownership more carefully, which has a positive impact on architecture. The arena pattern everywhere A few years ago I analyzed a bunch of XML tree libraries in Rust. The best I found, roxmltrree , has an immutable tree. But I needed a mutable tree. I found quite a few libraries that did support mutability, but many did not support parent references. You couldn't walk up the ancestor chain of a node. This, along with missing support for some XML features, is why I created my own in the form of Xot . The reason for this surprising lack of parent references is the ownership limitation I discussed before: Rust makes circular references difficult. You can get around it using reference counted types and internal mutability, but in a lot of cases this pattern isn't really optimal -- it's verbose, less performant, and reference count cycles risk memory leaks. What you do instead is store nodes in an array and you use the array indexes to node as your reference. You can then have an index referencing your parent, and use index references to your children, or any other circular reference. A fancy word for this pattern is an 'arena' and in Rust they show up everywhere. In an arena, you store a lot of objects together in the same region of memory (in an array). What does it let you do? iterate fast over its contents. Objects being in the same memory region means the CPU can use its cache effectively. This is much faster than arbitrary main memory access and loops really benefit. fast allocation. The arena is allocated from the heap as a block, and after that your allocations may just be a few increments. interning: you store something once in the arena and use it in many places, so you don't duplicate data. the arena owns its stuff. Everything in the arena has the same lifetime. Indexes between objects in an arena can be circular without worrying. Rust pushes you to use arenas. This involves more ceremony than just using a direct reference, but it also means Rust pushes you to write code that computers can execute really efficiently. Performance has a quality all its own I mentioned performance a number of times. But what about premature optimization ? The great irony of this quote is that it comes from a paper where the author, Knuth, argues in favor of keeping the goto statement around, as it's essential for writing efficient software. Rust lets you know what you pay for. Reference counting? Dynamic dispatch? You can do it, but it's going to be visible in your code. Rust also often lets you know when you don't want to pay for it: just look at tower middleware and despair about all the generic types and type constraints that get piled onto a relatively simple abstraction. When you have these tools available, need to develop new wisdom about tradeoffs that never seemed to matter. If you write Python code you're not too worried about hash tables being a performance bottle neck, but in Rust code they certainly can be. You can get lost along the way into hyper optimization land. Often you need to just get go 8 . Many patterns that are just plain readable Rust code anyway happen to also be friendly to the CPU executing it. But Rust overwhelming you with details you may not want to think about is not the whole story, because performance is not just quantitative: if your code can truly be more performance, it can access new qualities. When you can write code that uses no memory and no CPU time 9 , it changes how you think. It changes what's possible. Sometimes the quality of performance is obvious: if you write numerical code, or a simulation, of course you don't want to wait for the answer. Being able to do many computations really fast is key to making AI possible. But it's more subtle that that: modern computers are really powerful, and ridicously fast, and we generally ignore that and just throw more resources at our problems. There are good reasons why this happens . But if we open our eyes a little, there are new architectural possibilities we can explore. While the power of macros were the biggest language surprise, I think this is the biggest shift in my thinking: access to performance unlocks possibilities I hadn't considered before. Take my experiment Colchis : a library can store vast amounts of JSON in memory, while retaining full access, even indexed access (I still hope to add jsonpath one day!), to JSON data. Before Rust, this was a possibility that wasn't even on my radar. Rust made me a better programmer because I can make the computer do more with less, opening up new areas of opportunity. Conclusion Rust is one of the most difficult programming languages I've learned -- and thus one of the languages that changed me the most. There's a simple part of Rust that isn't much harder to manage than any language, and in some cases may actually make your life easier -- enum s, declarative type-driven frameworks, and the excellent dev tooling come to mind. Even arenas are fundamentally not that difficult to understand. The complexity is in unlearning some habits and learning new ones. And then there's a more challenging complex Rust, mostly, but not always under the surface, there when you need it. Rust expands the reach of what I can build. That's what makes me happy I went on this journey. 10 1 AI agents write a lot of code. They know the programming language, so do you need to know it? Does the language still affect the developer? If you share my belief it's good to look at the code , then it helps if you understand the code you're reading. I also think it's never been more important to think about how the systems you use affect the way you think and behave. 2 If you don't know what a struct is, just call it a class in your head, and you're good. 3 You have them in many languages but in impoverished forms, like true / false , or C's enum . 4 If you're going to do static type checking anyway for the guarantees it brings, perhaps use a language designed around it (enums!) that also gives you performance benefits? 5 Does AI truly understand? Do you want to have a philosophical debate? What do we mean by understand ? Natural language is inherently stretchable . 6 With AI we've seen the return of big design up front. I may be wrong, but I'm still skeptical of this approach, and still a fan of iterative development and incremental learning and theory building. 7 Not impossible. I've seen it. People can do it if they really try, and it still makes life harder; it makes it much harder to test. But at least it's more obvious and more difficult to do. 8 Clone and own all the stuff! Which incidentally can also lead to more contiguous memory layouts... 9 No memory and no CPU time is an exaggeration, but little Rust programs sometimes feel that way. 10 AI development is shifting all the tradeoffs in software development - they're not gone, but they have shifted. The AI can write Rust, even if you don't know it. But I trust plenty of contexts remain where my Rust experience plus AI leads to a better outcome than AI by itself. ←  Prev Coding with a Sigh Copied! Follow A widespread, yet short-lived, system outage at United Airlines on Monday delayed some outbound flights at US airports, the airline told CNN in a statement, coming on the heels of a rare FAA ground stop that caused massive disruption . The outage lasted about 30 minutes, with fewer than 150 flights impacted, United Airlines spokesperson Leslie Scott told CNN. United acknowledged the issue just before 5 p.m. ET, saying the technology outage was impacting departing flights, and an hour later the airline announced it had been resolved. “While some flights were delayed, there was no impact on flights in progress, or on United Express flights,” United Airlines said in a statement. During the incident, the FAA said United was experiencing a technology outage on its end and that “it’s not an FAA equipment issue.” Related article CNN ‘Working on floppy disks’: FAA has fielded years of warnings about old systems 7 min read United said there is no indication that the outage was a cybersecurity-related issue. The technology outage affected access to multiple applications used by flight crews, according to an internal company alert obtained by CNN. The airline instructed pilots not to log out of several systems, warning they may be unable to sign back in. The affected applications included flight planning, weather briefing and crew management tools. Pilots unable to access their flight plans were being directed to contact dispatchers to have the documents emailed to them. The memo did not disclose the cause of the outage. Air traffic control audio captured by ATC.com shows the moment the outage occurred. “Hey, we’re uh, still waiting on our final weights,” a pilot on United Flight 1728 in El Paso, heading to Denver, said to a controller. “We just contacted ops and apparently there’s a company-wide system outage on it so might be a while.” The controller responds back, “United 1728, roger, so you don’t have any idea when you think you’ll be able to leave?” “No ma’am,” the pilot responds. Aviation industry still recovering from weekend ground stop The industry had largely returned to normal operations after the nationwide ground stop was lifted just after 8 p.m. ET on Friday, though airlines have still worked to reposition planes, crews and luggage as they grappled with the weekend’s score of cancellations and delays . Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy held a 45-minute news conference Saturday morning to address the FAA ground stop, and apologized to travelers as he said he was still working to determine what exactly went wrong. Related article A traveler waits in line at John F. Kennedy International Airport in New York on November 14. Ryan Murphy/Getty Images With the busiest travel season ahead, how likely is it that another FAA ground stop happens? 8 min read Duffy told reporters that upgrade work on an old telecommunication system could be a cause for Friday’s nationwide ground stop. In at least one remote FAA location, Duffy said contractor L3Harris was doing routine maintenance to switch telecommunication lines from an old copper wire to fiber, which he described as “straightforward” work that has been happening across the country for decades. As United Airlines indicated for Monday’s system outage, Friday’s ground stop didn’t appear to have been caused by a cyber attack or any “nefarious” activity, Duffy stressed at the news conference. “A lot of questions came in yesterday. ‘Was this a, a cyber attack? Did some foreign nation attack this network?’ And the answer to that is we don’t believe so,” Duffy said. This story has been updated with additional information. On Call Supercomputing REG AD saas Microsoft blames monster email outage on software defect introduced in July fix Summer code change caused a Fall fail – frantic engineers had to patch the patch instead of rolling back Richard Speed Richard Speed MICROSOFT ECOSYSTEM REPORTER Published mon 16 Nov 2026 // 11:15 UTC Make us preferred on Google READ MORE Microsoft fixes Windows activation as admins pick through Exchange outage wreckage 8 hours ago Microsoft Outlook outage blamed after 15 injured in hotel pool chlorine incident 10 hours ago We don't need no education platform evolution. Hey, Redmond, leave those kids alone 16 hours ago Microsoft’s Azure Linux dons Fedora to dress itself up for mainstream workloads 19 hours ago Microsoft lifts Indian cloud prices by 15 percent, cuts costs in China 1 day ago Microsoft has blamed last week's epic outage on a change it made in July that lurked in the network gateway servers until a surge in load and a drop in capacity triggered the defect, giving the Microsoft 365 world a day off from email. According to a preliminary post incident report published by Microsoft on November 15, the defect was introduced in July 2026. The update looked fine at the time, Microsoft says, having passed load testing and been deployed without any impact. However, the testing wasn't good enough. Microsoft's report states: "Our load testing tended to focus on weaker hardware with fewer cores." The defect caused "lock contention inside an internal Windows process which caused the machine's resources (CPU & memory) to be exhausted." REG AD "The contention issue is worsened on machines with more cores and newer hardware." REG AD The fix containing the defect was prepared specifically for Microsoft 365 network gateway servers. Then two things happened at once. Teams failed over to the "primary" gateway that supports Exchange Online, creating a surge in load that was not, in itself, particularly unusual. At the same time, almost 14 percent of server capacity for the networking gateway was out of service, which wasn't a problem by itself either: it was on its way to being restored and, according to Microsoft, "the service had sufficient capacity headroom." Together, they pushed the gateway into the defect and chaos ensued.  It was a classic cascading failure scenario. When a server loses connectivity, traffic gets routed to the next healthy endpoint. Which encountered the same problem. So traffic was rerouted again and… you can see where this was going. Within two hours, the defect was encountered across Microsoft's fleet. "At its lowest," the report states, "more than 80 percent of servers were unresponsive." So, what to do? Bringing servers back to service didn't help – they were immediately overwhelmed and fell over again. "Our normally automated recovery processes were not designed to restore service from this broad unresponsive state." A straightforward rollback was also not possible because the defect was months old. Instead, engineers developed patch for the patch or, in Microsoft's words, "an update that returned the code path to the previously known good state in Windows." The patch was applied to groups of servers and service was gradually restored. The timings show the pain customers experienced and the floundering in Redmond as Microsoft tried to work out why Exchange Online and other cloud services were so poorly. The Teams failover, which turned out to be a factor in the outage, happened at 0107 UTC on November 12. During the day, the load began to ramp up until, at 1603 UTC, Microsoft's connectivity anomaly detection monitor identified an increase in connectivity issues. At 1633 UTC, the first support case came in. It is not difficult to imagine the stress engineers felt as, over the next 15 hours, nothing they tried resolved the issue. All ongoing and planned deployments and configuration changes were paused while the team attempted to resurrect the service. Extra capacity was added. Traffic was rerouted. Yet servers kept falling over. REG AD "Those services that were able – like Teams, OneDrive, SharePoint, and Office apps – failed out of the faulty network gateway infrastructure," the report says. "But not all services, like Exchange Online, can fail out of this network gateway for scale reasons." Hence the length of time for which Exchange Online (or, from the perspective of many users, Outlook) was out of action. By 0030 UTC on November 13, Microsoft had identified connection negotiation as the main culprit for the access failures and concluded that competing processes were preventing connections from being handled. However, it took until 0720 UTC before "We identified a mitigation and applied the mitigation –  an update that reverted the defective change." At 1610 UTC, Microsoft confirmed that things were once again looking healthy and, at 0415 on November 14, issued its final customer update. A final post incident report is due on November 20. However, the preliminary report will do little to calm jangling nerves. An update applied three months ago managed to cause Exchange Online (and other services) disruption on a global scale? With load testing that didn't reflect scenarios under Microsoft's control? The engineers who worked feverishly to restore services deserve commendation and will hopefully never have to buy their own beverages in Redmond again (or at least escape the next round of firings). However, the processes that led to an update with a latent defect reaching production deserve a long, hard look. ® outlook microsoft saas outage Make us preferred on Google REG AD 350 tech jobs hammered as TCS takes over work at iconic Australian retailer Bunnings Warehouse needs a technology model its current employees somehow can’t deliver US extends chip sale restrictions to more Asian countries to reduce risk of ‘diversion’ to China 'Know Your Customer's Workload' requirements imposed on cloud operators across Asia, Brazil Has AI’s ‘Black October’ changed the way you secure your code? title: Many of Amazon’s Black Friday and Cyber Monday “deals” offered no savings
body_text: Amazon’s Decoy Deals: Groundwork Investigation Reveals Nearly 1 in 3 Black Friday and Cyber Monday “Deals” Advertised by Amazon Offered No Savings to Shoppers, Nearly 1 in 10 Were Actually More Expensive - Groundwork Collaborative Menu Who We Are What We Do In The News Our Team Join Us Contact Us Gouged Amazon’s Decoy Deals: Groundwork Investigation Reveals Nearly 1 in 3 Black Friday and Cyber Monday “Deals” Advertised by Amazon Offered No Savings to Shoppers, Nearly 1 in 10 Were Actually More Expensive November 16, 2026 Amazon’s Decoy Deals: Groundwork Investigation Reveals Nearly 1 in 3 Black Friday and Cyber Monday “Deals” Advertised by Amazon Offered No Savings to Shoppers, Nearly 1 in 10 Were Actually More Expensive A blockbuster new investigation from Groundwork Collaborative exposes how Amazon shoppers may be getting hosed during the retail giant’s much-touted Black Friday and Cyber Monday sale events . The report, Deal or Decoy? Amazon’s Deceptive Discounts , examines products the retailer showcased as some the “best” discounts of the year to shoppers hunting for bargains during these sale events. A closer look at hundreds of these “deals” finds that Amazon frequently offered shoppers the same price, or in some cases a higher price, during recent holiday sale events than they could have paid just weeks earlier. The report’s authors, Breyon Williams, Elizabeth Pancotti, and Lindsay Owens, find that nearly 1 in 3 of these Amazon “deals” offered no real savings – the exact same products were sold for the same price or less in the month before the sale. During Black Friday and Cyber Monday sales in the past two years, prices for nearly 1 in 10 products advertised as “deals” were higher than what customers could have paid for the products in the month leading up to the sales. Groundwork’s analysis examined the prices of more than 350 products included on Amazon’s own deal pages for the Black Friday and Cyber Monday sale events in 2024 and 2025. These pages promote these deals as some of the “best” deals available. Amazon’s Black Friday 2025 deals page says, “With so many deals to explore, we’ve handpicked some of the best ones you’ll find.” Groundwork Collaborative President and CEO and report co-author Lindsay Owens , shared the following reaction: “Millions of Americans wait all year for Black Friday and Cyber Monday to score the biggest bargains on stocking stuffers and household staples. Shoppers trust that the deals advertised to them deliver real savings because Amazon promotes them that way. But it turns out that these major sales aren’t all they’re cracked up to be. Instead, our investigation reveals that shoppers who wait for these major sale events may be playing rip-off roulette. “Amazon dominates online shopping, and families count on its sale events to stretch their dollars. With the holiday shopping season upon us and prices continuing to rise, shoppers deserve to know they can trust every deal Amazon promises them. If Amazon can’t deliver that basic promise, lawmakers should hold them accountable.” Owens is the author of the recent book Gouged: The End of a Fair Price—And What That Means for Your Wallet , which exposes how corporations are sophisticated pricing schemes to overcharge consumers. The report’s key findings include: The price of nearly 1 in 3 products that Amazon described as “deals” was the same – or higher – during sale events than what customers could have purchased them for in the month leading up to the sale. Some Amazon “deals” offered shoppers higher prices than they could have paid before the sale. On Black Friday 2025, a pair of yellow Hunter Women’s Short Rain Boots “on sale” for $126.99 had been $79.97 nine days before the sale event started, meaning customers looking for a deal could’ve paid 59% more if they waited for the sale. On Cyber Monday 2025, a pair of men’s UGG Butte boots “on sale” for $179.98 had been $98.40 roughly four weeks before the start of the sale event, meaning the “deal” cost 83% more than the recent low. Among these “worse” deals, the median sale-event price was 19% higher than what shoppers could have paid for the products in the weeks leading up to the sale. Since learning of our study, Amazon has removed the aforementioned deal pages our study drew from, but archived versions of these pages can be found at the following links: Black Friday 2024 , Cyber Monday 2024 , Black Friday 2025 , Cyber Monday 2025 . Amidst the ongoing affordability crisis, millions of Americans count on holiday sale events, like Black Friday, to deliver real savings. In 2025, a record 203 million Americans shopped between Thanksgiving and Cyber Monday, and this year, 70% of U.S. customers plan to take advantage of holiday promotions. Deal or Decoy calls on federal and state regulators to crack down on misleading discounts and require retailers to show the lowest price a product sold for in the previous 30 days when advertising a sale. ADDITIONAL BACKGROUND The new report builds on Groundwork’s work exposing corporate pricing abuses and delivering results for American consumers. In December 2025, Groundwork teamed up with Consumer Reports and More Perfect Union to expose how Instacart was charging shoppers different prices for the exact same groceries at the same store and time. The findings made national headlines , triggered investigations by the Federal Trade Commission and New York Attorney General , and prompted Instacart to end the practice just weeks later. Following the publication of Groundwork’s Owens’ book Gouged: The End of a Fair Price—And What That Means for Your Wallet , the Federal Trade Commission launched an investigation into major retailers’ use of customers’ personal data to set prices, adding to growing scrutiny of corporate pricing practices and their impact on Americans’ wallets in response to Groundwork and Owens’ research. In October 2026, Groundwork exposed Walmart’s creepy patent filings and pricing playbook. The report digs into patent filings, privacy disclosures, and technology investments to reveal how the retailer is building the infrastructure that could allow it to deploy personalized pricing at scale. title: Interpreting claims that a theorem is correct because it was checked in Lean
body_text: “…and the proof is checked in Lean” | Xena Xena Mathematicians learning Lean by doing. Skip to content Home About Xena Student projects Installing Lean and mathlib Bluesky Useful links. ← A Modern Reorganization of Mathematics “…and the proof is checked in Lean” Posted on November 12, 2026 by xenaproject This post is an attempt to explain in simple terms how to interpret claims of the form “this theorem is correct because it was checked in Lean”. The summary is: there is an important signal that can be extracted from Lean code, but if this code is AI-generated then you need to do some tests first. We explain the tests, and note that in many cases (such as the OpenAI theorem dump) these tests have not yet been systematically done. Introduction Last month’s theorem dump by OpenAI consisted of 722 mathematics papers, around 45% of which came with some Lean code. Three of the (non-Leanified) papers have since been retracted because of a sign error. Some people might say “well, the papers that come with Lean code are definitely correct because that’s how Lean works”. Others might say “well Lean had a soundness bug and could well have more, and AIs will reward hack, so Lean verification doesn’t tell us much at all”. The truth, unsurprisingly, is more subtle, and this post is an attempt to explain it. This post is structured as a sequence of four questions that one needs to ask about a Lean repository, particularly if it is AI-generated, before one can start to make correctness claims of this form. And before I start, let me stress that for many of the papers in the OpenAI theorem dump, these questions have not yet all been answered affirmatively (but there is nothing stopping people from answering these questions, and I have no reason to believe that any of the tests below will fail, it’s just that people didn’t do them yet). Question 1. Does the Lean statement match the informal statement? A Lean repository will typically have a “headline theorem statement”. This will be some computer code which defines the statement (not the proof!) of a theorem. Note the huge difference here between the statement, and the proof. For example here is some fully-compiling Lean code which defines a mathematical statement. import Mathlib def FermatsLastTheorem : Prop := ∀ a b c n : ℕ, n ≥ 3 → a^n + b^n ≠ c^n This code imports Lean’s mathematics library Mathlib and then defines a mathematical statement which looks at first glance like it might be Fermat’s Last Theorem, but which actually is a trivially false statement because in Lean ℕ contains 0 , so a = b = c = 0 and n = 3 gives a counterexample. This does not stop the statement from compiling! It will however stop any proof of this statement from compiling. Lean carefully distinguishes between the statement of a theorem and the proof of a theorem; humans are very good at referring to both ideas as “a theorem”. The first question which one has to ask when judging a pdf which comes with some Lean code is: “what is the statement of the theorem in the Lean code, and does this correspond to the actual theorem statement in the pdf?” For a human Lean expert, this is typically (but not always) an easy question to answer. For example any Lean-competent human mathematician would be able to read the two lines of code above and observe that this was a mis-statement of Fermat’s Last Theorem. Things are, however, not always as easy as this. Currently, because of deficiencies in available libraries, one may have to read many thousands of lines of code just to understand the statement of a formalised theorem. An example of this right now is a PR to DeepMind’s Formal Conjectures repository containing a Lean formalisation of the statement of the Hodge conjecture. At the time of writing, the statement relies on over 10,000 lines of code sitting on top of Mathlib , because Mathlib (which is carefully human-expert-checked and which can be trusted) does not yet have the definitions of things like the cycle class map needed to make the statement. Another example is Axiom’s recent announcement of a formally-verified proof of the classification of finite simple groups . The statement which Axiom’s system proved is here in Tau Ceti, an AI-generated library of Lean code. The file containing the statement imports over 250K lines of Lean code in Tau Ceti (over 900 files). Of these, around 5600 lines of code are crucial because they contain all the relevant definitions (for example, all the definitions of the sporadic simple groups, most of which are still not in Mathlib ). Without human checking, one does not really know for sure that this is definitely the correct statement of the classification (and note that I have not yet met any human who claims to have carefully checked that the definitions of the sporadic groups in Tau Ceti are correct). In fact by far the strongest evidence that we have that this statement is correctly formalized is that Axiom’s code proves it! It is worth noting that of the 290 OpenAI theorems which come with Lean code, around 38 of them have the property that the Lean code does not even state, let alone prove, the main theorem of the paper . And OpenAI never claimed that it did! They just said “here is some Lean code which goes with this paper”. Sometimes the code just states and proves some intermediate results — my impression is that OpenAI decided to go live when some of the formalizations were incomplete, so just dumped what they had. To give a concrete example: paper 194 claims to prove Lech’s multiplicity conjecture in commutative algebra, with no restriction on dimension, residue field or characteristic; this question has been open since 1960. The headline theorem in the corresponding Lean code can be checked to be Corollary 5.4 of the paper — already an impressive achievement, but not the headline result. Question 2: does the code compile? Once you’re convinced that you understand the statement of the theorem which the Lean code purports to prove, you (or perhaps one of your friends who has access to a beefy machine, if the code base is huge) has to actually compile the code. When Anthropic formalized a proof of Fermat’s Last Theorem in Lean , they asked me to take a look at the 13 million lines of code which they had generated. I downloaded it onto my machine, dumped it into a sandbox (because who knows what AI-generated code will do, it can in theory delete all your files) and attempted to compile it; I very quickly ran out of memory. I told Anthropic that I was unable to make any claims about what they had done until I could see the code base compiling, and they gave me temporary access to a machine with 96 cores and 500 gigs of ram. I could then compile the code. Of course, with a more reasonably-sized codebase it is possible to compile the code on a reasonably-sized machine. For example OpenAI’s resolution of the Navier-Stokes problem is 640K lines of code and compiles fine on my laptop. It is probably worth stressing again: do not run random Lean code on your local machine unless you sandbox it first. Lean’s mathematics library is safe to run and build upon because this is human-curated and checked by human experts. AI-generated code is not. Question 3: does the code prove the theorem as stated? I already talked in Question 1 about the importance of checking the statement of a theorem, so we can be sure that the code is proving the right thing. However, there is an added complication here. Ideally the statement of a theorem will be contained in a file which has very few imports beyond Mathlib , so we know we can trust it. But the proof of the theorem will necessarily import thousands and possibly millions of lines of code which nobody wants to read. How do we know for sure that there is no trick hidden in the millions of lines of proof files which redefines x^n to mean 37 , and then proves that a^n + b^n ≠ c^n because the left hand side is 37+37=74 and the right hand side is 37 ? Or which adds a new axiom to mathematics saying that the theorem is true? Put another way — given a Challenge.lean file with only trusted code imported and the statement of a theorem, and a Solution.lean file with millions of lines of untrusted code imported and the proof of a theorem which looks identical , how do we know for sure that somewhere in the millions of lines of code there is no hack which changes the meaning of the statement, changes the rules from just the axioms of mathematics, The one-line answer: lake comparator . You can read more about this answer here . But in short, this tool checks that the theorem stated in a trusted file and the theorem proved via untrusted imports are identical, and that only the axioms of mathematics are used in the proof. Question 4: does the code exploit a bug in Lean’s official kernel? This can happen. There was a soundness bug in Lean’s kernel which was fixed four hours after it was discovered, and a subsequent review of Lean’s code base by OpenAI found several more, all of which were fixed before they were announced publicly. There may in theory be more soundness bugs in Lean’s kernel. However, this does not matter . Why not? Because Lean now has many kernels, created by users, written in many different languages, and at least one of which is formally verified to have no bugs, right down to the assembly level. If you want to make absolutely sure that there is no reward-hacking then again there is a one-line answer: lake comparator --paranoid . A malicious piece of code exploiting an as-yet-undiscovered bug in Lean’s official kernel will not pass this test unless it exploits as-yet-undiscovered bugs in many independent systems all at once. For example this webpage from the Lean kernel arena demonstrates that OpenAI’s resolution of the Navier–Stokes problem is accepted by multiple kernels as well as Lean’s official kernel. One final remark Even if the Lean code compiles and passes all these tests, and is thus overwhelmingly likely to be a correct proof of a theorem, this does not mean that any corresponding pdf also contains a correct proof! The Navier–Stokes lost in translation paper demonstrates the opposite in fact, for the Navier-Stokes write-up; whilst all the tests above have been run for the Navier–Stokes work, there are instances where the pdf proof and the Lean proof diverge. In these cases, who knows if the pdf proof is OK! My understanding is that some experts have been using AI to informalise the Lean proof back into English in order to read the argument, rather than ploughing through the slop in the pdf. Summary/conclusions “It’s true because it’s checked in Lean” can be made to make sense. But one has to do some work beyond “the Lean code compiles”. Your frontier AI model can do all of this work. But it needs to be done, and (depending on the amount of Lean code in the proof) it may be computationally costly. (is the verification in some other proof assistant? couldn’t there be a soundness bug in that?) Like Like Reply xenaproject says: November 12, 2026 at 8:17 am I think I’ll defer to the master and just point you to https://leodemoura.github.io/blog/2026-10-15-lean-now-ships-with-verified-kernels/ Like Like Reply coolio says: November 12, 2026 at 1:48 pm Thanks, I’d seen that blog post, but as someone who doesn’t know much about Lean, it’s a bit hard to interpret, and I’m interested in why *you* find it reassuring. title: The Secret ThinkPad Powerbutton Code to Bring Dead Laptops Back to Life (2007)
body_text: The Secret Thinkpad Powerbutton Code To Bring Dead Laptops Back To Life | Mike Masnick Mike Masnick Blog About Search Techdirt   The Secret Thinkpad Powerbutton Code To Bring Dead Laptops Back To Life Mike Masnick · September 7, 2007 Permalink Two months ago, I got a new laptop. It’s a Lenovo Thinkpad z61t. I actually ordered a t61, but I accidentally got the z61 instead — and, I actually really like it. It’s quite similar to the t61, but a little smaller and lighter. I was worried that the smaller part would be a problem, but I’ve gotten used to it. I really like the fact that it’s much lighter than my old t42. It just makes it seem so much more usable on the go. Lugging out the t42 was always a chore. Anyway, I was at the Office 2.0 conference today, where I was giving a little presentation on the Techdirt Insight Community, and about an hour before the presentation, I went to find a quiet place to practice the presentation… and discovered that my brand new laptop wouldn’t work. I knew something was wrong when the “sleep” light wasn’t lit. I started to get worried when I plugged in the laptop and the battery light didn’t light up. Then I noticed that even though the machine had been asleep, it was really really hot. Pushing the power button did nothing. No lights were on and nothing seemed to get them to turn on. I pulled out the battery and put it back in and that did nothing as well. So I called up IBM support and explained the situation. The guy on the other end then let me in on the secret power button code to revive your dead Thinkpad. After assessing the situation (totally dead laptop) he warned me: “Okay, this is going to sound totally bizarre, but I want you to give this a try…” He then had me unplug the AC adapter and take out the battery. Then, you push the power button 10 times in a row at one second intervals. Next, you push and hold the power button for 30 seconds. Then you put the battery back in and push the power button… and she lives. The computer came back, good as ever. I asked the guy what the power button pushing incantation did and he said “static discharge” so apparently there was some sort of static that caused a short or something. I tried to get the guy to explain in more detail what happened, but he said “dude, you know as much as I do… but your machine is working.” And so it is. So, if you happen to have a Thinkpad that suddenly drops completely dead for no reason, try the power button trick. Forget up, up, down, down, left, right, left, right, B, A. WCR on September 10th, 2014 1st off this works on any laptop/model not just think-pad. This isn’t a magic trick, the point of this besides the static discharge, this resets the Bios of computer by pulling all the charge out of the Internal 2032 CMOS Battery, which in return reboots the BIOS. This can happen for many reason not just a static charge, Some computers can have a bad infection that activates when the computer goes to sleep mode, this is a well known attacker, then the virus proceeds to overload your machine to shut down thus causing the bios to have the command programmed to stay shut down. Well by doing the manual BIOS RESET such as this, resets the configurations in the bios back to default. Also you can try pulling battery out, unplugging charger, and then hold power button for 1 minute if the 10X an 30sec hold doesn’t work for you. And if for some reason it still don’t work, removing the 2032 CMOS Battery on the MOBO for 1 minute or replace it, the battery which is usually located near the RAM on most laptops, not all have the battery located in same place, I suggest if you need to go that far google your model of computer to locate the internal CMOS Battery. title: Nvidia was in trouble before the Jensen Huang mess
body_text: Nvidia Was Already in Trouble Before the Jensen Huang Mess | WIRED Skip to main content THE WIRED APP IS HERE DOWNLOAD NOW » Menu WIRED SECURITY POLITICS THE BIG STORY BUSINESS SCIENCE CULTURE REVIEWS Menu WIRED Account Account Newsletters Security Politics The Big Story Business Science Culture Reviews Chevron More Expand The Big Interview Magazine Events WIRED Insider WIRED Consulting Newsletters Podcasts Video Livestreams WIRED Store Search Search Will Knight Business Nov 16, 2026 6:00 AM Nvidia Was Already in Trouble Before the Jensen Huang Mess AI competitors are catching up to Nvidia—and poised to take advantage of the chaos. Photo-Illustration: Wired Staff; Getty Images Comment Loader Save Story Save this story Comment Loader Save Story Save this story Nvidia played a key role enabling the AI gold rush thanks in large part to its recently ousted CEO Jensen Huang . Huang was a master of foreseeing technological changes , investing in chips to train AI earlier than most. But just as he’s leaving , the company has a growing list of competitors with a range of new, advanced technology breathing down its neck. For Nvidia , where CFO Colette Kress has now taken the reins, the timing isn’t great. “Everything sold today was designed two to three years ago,” says the CEO of a large AI company, who spoke to WIRED on condition of anonymity to avoid hurting business relationships. Kress, or whoever replaces her permanently, will have to chart the course that the chip industry will take two years from now, the CEO says. Already, competitors have started to move in. Nvidia dominates the market for AI accelerators, capturing 80 percent of sales, according to Silicon Analysis. Longtime nemesis AMD is now making a concerted effort to build competitive AI chips. Its share of the market has crept up from just two percent in 2022 to between 7 and 10 percent in 2026. Big US cloud players—Google, Amazon, and Microsoft—are all developing more specialized chips to power the training and serving of AI models. Each has seen similar gains. These companies are designing their own silicon to reduce costs and to gain some independence from Nvidia. Several startups now offer more specialized chips that promise improvements over Nvidia’s core products. Cerebras, for instance, sells giant ones meant to power giant AI models. AMD recently bought Taalas, a company that burns models’ weights into silicon to make computations ultra efficient. Using these chips requires rewriting a lot of code, however, to make them work with cutting-edge AI models. Patrick Moorhead, chief analyst at MoorInStrat, a company that tracks the chip industry, says the rise of AI agents makes inference, or running models that have already been trained, more important. That’s an area where Nvidia has less of an edge compared to cloud hyperscalers and startups. Nvidia did, however, acquire a startup making specialized chips, called Groq, in December of 2025. And because of the rise in AI assistants and agents, there’s also growing demand for general purpose central processing units (CPUs), Moorhead said, an area where Nvidia barely competes. Nvidia still maintains a huge lead in AI thanks to Huang’s foresight. Huang cofounded the company in 1993 to design graphics chips for PCs. In the mid-2010s, he saw the promise of AI. He funded academic research on the topic, developed software to support AI engineering, and gave hardware to labs and startups. In 2022, ChatGPT took AI mainstream and sales of Nvidia chips skyrocketed. The company’s revenue went from $26.91 billion in January 2022 to $215.94 billion in January 2026. The challenges it faces may not be existential—but they do add up, especially on a global scale. China Challenge While Nvidia’s fortunes have risen in the US, they have declined in the world’s other big market for AI: China. Washington is trying to restrict access to its most advanced chips, while Beijing is trying to develop its own chip industry. Nvidia is not allowed to sell its most powerful chips in China, but it can sell previous generations. Sales of these chips as well as non AI chips doubled over the past year, but China now accounts for only eight percent of the company’s overall revenue, compared with 20 percent in 2024, according to its fillings. It remains unclear how many chips exported to other countries may either end up in China or end up being used remotely by Chinese firms. Huawei, a Chinese tech giant targeted with US sanctions for several years, has developed new kinds of supercomputers that harness many more chips than usual to train and run AI models. Some Chinese AI companies, such as Z.ai, which makes one of the world’s best open source models, say they’ve trained their models entirely using Huawei’s chips. If Chinese open-weight models gain traction in other countries, it could create a market for Chinese chips elsewhere. Huang’s dealings with China played a major role in his downfall. He had a romantic relationship with Huang Le, also known as Alice Huang, a Chinese executive at a Singaporean company called Megaspeed who the US government suspects of being an asset of China’s Ministry of State Security. Megaspeed and its subsidiaries have reportedly imported between $4.6 and $7.5 billion Nvidia chips into southeast Asia. Reports suggest that the company may have provided access to the chips to Chinese AI firms. Babak Minovi, a senior analyst at the Eurasia Group, a consultancy that focuses on technology and geopolitics, says Huang was right to point out that cutting off access to China would empower domestic rivals. “Huang was taking a pragmatic line, and he knows competition,” he says. Trend Spotting Even in markets that it dominates, Nvidia may turn out to be a victim of its own success. The AI models built using Nvidia’s chip are automating the very elements of coding, data analysis, and scientific research that help design chips. Most chip design firms use specialized AI models to arrange components on processors—something that traditionally required deep engineering expertise and experience. And both OpenAI and Anthropic have recently touted the ability of their newest models to design electronics from scratch. Moorhead says the shift towards AI chip design may not pose a huge threat to Nvidia because it’s riding the same wave. “They have access to AI too,” he notes. But Moorhead says the way AI models can now quickly rewrite code to run on different hardware may prove a problem. For years, Nvidia has attracted developers by providing software that makes it easy to write programs and build models for its silicon. Its Compute Unified Device Architecture, or CUDA, has long been seen as a moat to ensure AI companies continue to rely on Nvidia chips. But AI models are now so good at reading and writing code that they can port an AI model over to a competitor's silicon at speed. Wafer, a startup that uses AI to port models to AMD and then serves them more cheaply, has seen revenue grow spectacularly in recent months, boasts CEO Emilio Andere. Every time a major new open weight model is released Wafer can have it running on AMD hardware at least 80 percent as efficiently within hours, he says. Andere says AI is getting so capable that his engineers barely have to edit or review the code. Dan Hutchinson, a veteran chip analyst, says Nvidia may be entering its “Intel swan moment,” referring to the 2019 replacement of engineering-focused CEO Brian Krzanich with its CFO Bob Swan. ( Sound familiar ? Krzanich also resigned after a relationship with an employee; Huang is alleged to have had multiple.) From there, the company’s focus shifted to sales more than technical progress. Bureaucracy ballooned and revenue tanked. “Nvidia is now an Intel waiting to happen,” he says.
