title: Researchers track whole body movement with just a smartwatch
body_text: Researchers track whole body movement with just a smartwatch | Cornell Chronicle Skip to main content Toggle navigation Search Cornell University Cornell.edu Media Relations Search Cornell University Cornell Chronicle Topics Architecture & Design Artificial Intelligence Arts & Humanities Business, Economics & Entrepreneurship Computing & Information Sciences Energy, Environment & Sustainability Food & Agriculture Global Reach Health, Nutrition & Medicine Law, Government & Public Policy Life Sciences & Veterinary Medicine Physical Sciences & Engineering Social & Behavioral Sciences Research Matters Campus & Community News & Events Local Impact NYS Impact New York City Public Engagement Features Photos of the Week Student Life Staff News Big Red Sports Inclusion and Belonging University Statements In Memory Around Cornell All Stories Podcast Media Relations Cornellians Pause Video Researchers track whole body movement with just a smartwatch By Patricia Waldron Cornell Ann S. Bowers College of Computing and Information Science November 11, 2026 For the first time, researchers can track the movement of a person’s entire body with ultrasonic sound waves, using just an off-the-shelf smartwatch and a lightweight artificial intelligence model – all while ensuring privacy and efficiency. The new technology, called EchoMotion, was developed by Cornell’s  Smart Computer Interfaces for Future Interactions (SciFi) Lab , directed by Cheng Zhang , associate professor of information science in the Cornell Ann S. Bowers College of Computing and Information Science. It uses the built-in speaker and microphone on a commercial smartwatch to determine a person’s body position using a sonar-like sensing system. Once EchoMotion is integrated into commercial wearables or virtual reality (VR) systems, it could be used for tracking workouts, daily activities and progress on physical rehabilitation. EchoMotion represents a scalable approach that can use AI to understand human behaviors in the real world, Zheng said. He presented the paper, “ EchoMotion: Towards Full-Body Pose Tracking with a Single Smartwatch Using Active Acoustic Sensing ,” at the Association for Computing Machinery international joint conference on Pervasive and Ubiquitous Computing and International Symposium on Wearable Computing (UbiComp/IWSC), Oct. 13 in Shanghai. Credit: Provided Saif Mahmud, a Ph.D. candidate in the field of information science, demonstrates EchoMotion, a system for tracking body movements using an off-the-shelf smartwatch. “This is a very important jump for body tracking,” said Saif Mahmud, doctoral student in the field of information science and lead author of the new research. Existing wearable devices use sensors such as accelerometers and gyroscopes that determine the movement of the device alone, he said. As a result, whole body tracking traditionally has required more complicated setups that may also include smartphones, earbuds or VR headsets. Some tracking systems also integrate cameras, but EchoMotion’s use of sound waves offers multiple advantages. Acoustic signals preserve privacy for the wearer and the people around them – no need to set up a camera at the gym – and generate smaller amounts of data for easier and cheaper processing. “While large language models, like ChatGPT, have been in the news, EchoMotion shows how very small models running on wearables have also revolutionized sensing in human-computer interaction,” said co-author  François Guimbretière , professor of information science in Cornell Bowers. The technology also saves on battery power and works with existing off-the-shelf watches. In the prototype, sensing drew about 12 milliwatts, roughly 40 times less than a wearable camera, and a 30-minute session on a Galaxy Watch 6 used only 5% to 6% of the battery. “We have made significant efforts in making EchoMotion work on commercial devices, so that the adoption can be very easy,” Mahmud said. To develop the technology, the researchers initially created their own 3D-printed watch replica, which included a microphone and speaker pair on each side. The two speakers emit ultrasonic signals that surround a person in a sphere of inaudible sound waves. Then the two microphones pick up the echoes that bounce off the person’s limbs as they move. The researchers collected echo patterns from 10 volunteers who wore the watch on their nondominant hand as they performed 18 exercises. Using that data, the researchers developed a deep learning model to translate those patterns into body movements. They measured accuracy by comparing the predicted positions of 12 joints, from head to ankles, with the body poses captured by cameras. Off-the-shelf smartwatches have only a single microphone and speaker pair, however, so they tested the EchoMotion system on an unmodified Samsung Galaxy Watch 6 with 15 new volunteers. When used by people new to the system, the average error for predicting the location of each joint was under four inches. A one-time, 12-minute calibration cut that error by more than one third, to about 2.4 inches. The same AI model, without any retraining, also worked on a Samsung Galaxy Watch 7 and a Google Pixel Watch 3. To see how EchoMotion performed beyond the lab, the researchers asked 10 new participants to wear a smartwatch as they did the 18 exercises in a small room, in a narrow hallway and next to a noisy road. Furniture and ambient noise did not interfere, but the system’s performance suffered slightly in the hallway, due to echoes coming off of other people. Mahmud expects, however, that with more data – from thousands of users instead of dozens – their model will get better at interpreting a wearer’s movements even in crowded environments, like the subway. Currently, the team is developing the technology for use in fitness tracking, so a personal fitness agent will be able to count a user’s reps and even correct their form, for example, in a Bulgarian split squat. They are also exploring the use of EchoMotion in combination with first-person vision on smartglasses to efficiently track the objects that a person handles. “In the very near future, with wearables like smartwatches or smartglasses, a personal agent will write a description of your whole day – what you did, what you ate,” Mahmud said. “This project enables the body tracking part of that vision.” Co-authors on the study include Jiwan Kim of KAIST; Tianhong Catherine Yu, a doctoral student in the field of information science; Kenny Liang ’24 and Vineet Parikh ’20, M.S. ’24. The research was supported by the National Science Foundation. Patricia Waldron is a writer for the Cornell Ann S. Bowers College of Computing and Information Science. title: Software is breaking down at a systemic level
body_text: Software is breaking down at a systemic level | Jimmy Breck-McKye Jimmy Breck-McKye Blog About Software is breaking down at a systemic level 15 November 2026 opinion software ai Software hasn’t been working too well lately, has it? This weekend we saw the double-whammy of a 2 day global Microsoft outage, then an FAA ground-stop that halted all flights in the United States. Can you believe it’s only been four weeks since the PHP2Shell vulnerability? A critical exploit in PHP, powering an estimated 70% of the world’s websites, with sites taken completely offline as engineers frantically patched their systems. And then there was the eMudhra fiasco , where thousands of SSL certificates - the way we secure HTTPS websites and internet traffic - were compromised by a private key so weak, it was almost comical. It’s like 2026 has been a year of hacks, outages, vulnerabilities and IT panics. What exactly is going on here? You might be tempted to blame AI, and you wouldn’t be completely wrong. Artificial intelligence models are definitely a part of this. Even if companies like Microsoft don’t divulge whether broken systems were built with AI, we do know that hackers and researchers can now use AI technology to find complicated exploits in a matter of hours. I work with AI heavily in my job. It’s tremendously powerful. It’s also corrosive if used unwisely. But AI is both a cause and a symptom of the problem here. What we are seeing is software breaking down at a systemic level. This problem is insidious because it is not only the software itself that is broken, but the entire way we’ve come to build it. What does it mean for a failure to be systemic? Look at the recent crises in software reliability and you’ll notice they don’t share immediate causes - that we know of - yet they look uncannily similar to each other. Microsoft The Microsoft outage likely emerged from a network configuration failure that stopped MS datacenters communicating with each other. Exactly what happened next remains confidential, but it seems to have triggered a cascading failure where no service could be restored into a valid state long enough to bear traffic. Reddit and Bluesky speculated that even MSFT engineers had no real handle on the complexity of this outage. Microsoft have faced increasing criticism for the (un)reliability of their Azure platform. Back in March, ex-MSFT engineer Axel Rischin published this scathing criticism : Microsoft rushed Azure out of the gates under intense competitive pressure. Corners were cut. Fundamental principles of reliability and operational simplicity were quietly abandoned. Instead of going back to the drawing board to tackle the growing technical debt, Microsoft relied on quick fixes: layers of automation running mitigation scripts, a growing team of on-call staff, and, when automation was not enough, manual repairs. His article depicts a highly complex system made of low quality parts, where nobody can make sense of the whole picture. The PHP event On October 21st, security research firm Wiz proudly shared an exploit that could execute arbitrary code on any PHP website . Called PHP2Shell, Wiz trumpeted the power of AI tools to achieve exploits far beyond the skills of human attackers. It turns out the PHP runtime had hidden several complex memory bookkeeping bugs for over a decade. PHP is used extensively in e-commerce and most famously in WordPress, which was once the go-to for cheaply building simple websites. The PHP2Shell writeup depicts an internet dependent on a long chain of dependencies, hiding vulnerabilities too complex for any human to identify. Shai Hulud attack, May 2026 Most people outside of tech won’t have heard of this, but back in May we faced a crisis when an attacker compromised some important packages in the JavaScript ecosystem (NPM). These packages used GitHub Actions to perform Continuous Integration (CI) - automated tests, releases, etc. - and had a crucial misconfiguration where anyone who forked their projects could insert compromised code back upstream. When the next upstream CI build ran, it would retrieve libraries from a cache. The JavaScript package manager, NPM, allows these libraries to include scripts. They’re intended for housekeeping tasks, but here, they were used to hijack the projects’ secret tokens. The JavaScript ecosystem has long been criticised for poor security. NPM projects are complicated chains of dependencies calling dependencies calling dependencies. Any dependency may carry scripts. Any dependency author was just one slip away from allowing their code to be compromised - all they had to do was copy-paste the wrong code. In other words: a highly complex system made of low quality parts, where a single error can compromise everything. How we lost control It wasn’t always like this. Only 12 years ago, tech was a different industry. Building software was hard . Computer programs comprise millions of tiny instructions, and turning these into a workable system is like constructing a watch by hand, with hundreds of interacting components. Except, unlike a watch, each computer program must do something completely new and different. It was the most fun I’d had as an adult. It was as much an art as a science. You had to be able to hold everything in your head at once: visualise how all the tiny parts could be orchestrated into a cohesive whole. I recommend anyone the adventure of writing a computer program by hand. But, it was less fun if you were a manager. Not many people can write computer programs well, and it’s very hard to scale human beings. Getting them to communicate without misunderstandings is hard. Many projects failed. You can find programmers who know how to manage the complexity, but they want to be paid lots of money. Different movements attempted to solve the core problem. Some people thought that software development practices could help, like if you turned programming into highly structured templates of “best practices”. Or if you used management styles like SCRUM. But they only ever helped so much. About ten years ago, two small revolutions happened in our industry, whilst the rest of the world paid little attention. They were cloud computing, and open source libraries. Cloud computing was about substituting your hardware and infrastructure with virtualised infra you could rent from someone like Amazon Web Services. You could click a button in AWS and it was like a server just popped into existence by magic. Companies loved Cloud because it allowed them to remove sysadmins and ops people from the equation. You didn’t have to wait for someone to actually go to a site and install a rack in a datacenter. The promise was that your software could move as fast as code and not long after, a movement called DevOps essentially ended up merging developers and ops. And then, we had the Open Source boom. It was always possible to reuse code from other places - programmers sharing snippets on forums or sites like StackOverflow - but when tools like NPM hit the scene in 2014, it really felt like a gamechanger. You could just add a line to your package.json , hit npm install and - whoosh - now you could reuse code written by any stranger on the internet. Teams loved NPM (and PyPi, Maven…) because now they didn’t have to solve any hard problems if someone else had solved it first. All of the little components in a program - the cogs and wheels in my watchmaker analogy - were once crafted by hand. Now you could get cogs and wheels and whole mechanisms, for free, forever. This meant that the programmers could focus less on the details. Instead of figuring out the nitty gritty of, say, writing the code needed to check someone’s password, you could just ask NPM and friends to take care of it. Open source was great because you had a small number of passionate, unpaid developers, building code that everyone else depended on. You could make millions of dollars from their code, and you didn’t even have to be particularly nice to them. (People weren’t) But the cost was that everyone stopped knowing the details. You had to give away control. If an NPM package is compromised, or the author has an agenda, you’re in trouble. The cultural change Because there were fewer details to take care of, tech professionals began to lose their specialisms. You didn’t need a team of ops people, a team of backend developers, a team of mobile developers, a team of testers. You could flatten them into generalists. This changed the balance of power between workers and management. Imagine a building site where there is a plumber, a builder, and an electrician. If any one of them threatens to quit, you have a problem, because you need each of them to get the project done. Whereas if you can make everyone a mix of plumber-builder-electrician, they lose that leverage. Whether you think that power imbalance is a bad thing may depend on your politics. But it had a slow effect of taking influence away from the people close to the work. They’re the ones able to raise the alarm when things start going wrong. By 2016-17, there were signs that the superstructure of open source had weak points. The left-pad incident was an early warning of where we were going. In the tangled web of the JavaScript ecosystem, with its myriad dependencies, one library author took down his packages in a legal conflict, and ended up breaking almost everyone else’s projects. But largely we managed to make do. Even after the hiring and firing cycle of the post-pandemic era, and near misses like the XZ Utils backdoor , technology managed mostly to remain stable - thanks to armies of diligent developers and ops folk across the globe. And then AI came in …And, yes, then AI. A lot has been written about how AI systems are inherently non-deterministic, a kind of slot machine that only creates simulacra of work. Acting like a stochastic parrot, this argument goes, AI generated code will always be prone to hallucinations and bugs. And there’s truth to that. But I think the danger in the present moment is the opposite. It’s not so much that the model outputs are crap and unreliable. They’re actually pretty good at doing what you ask them to do (though I suspect that mostly works because Anthropic and co heavily subsidise compute). I think the real AI threat is decoherence . Kristen Maevyn wrote an essay named The Decoherence Trap which talks about a problem where the individual parts of a system may look fine in isolation, but don’t make sense as part of a larger system. Decoherence: the accumulation of locally valid but mutually incompatible or redundant models within a system, such that the cost of change is dominated by translating among those models and preventing unintended side-effects. Software engineers, as I’ve seen them working over the last year, have all but turned over all their work to AI agents. It started with small tasks like writing tests, functions, and individual components. But now it’s everything - not only the components, but the design, the orchestration, the whole concept. Programming was the activity of translating ideas and intents from the messy human world into code so crystalline, so precise and pedantic, that even a computer could execute it. It was fundamentally the act of distilling complexity into order, making something real out of nothing. This activity is rapidly dying. It no longer happens in most tech companies. Most SWEs now are unable to tackle engineering problems without some form of AI assistance. That’s not because they’re incompetent - they just can’t keep on top of the complexity. Even if they could once, they now face a tsunami of AI generated code. This is affecting everyone, at all levels - we are all fighting the tide of small, incoherent changes that look rational in isolation but slowly lose sense as a whole. Kristen writes: Decoherence grows relative to the rate of change of a system, and it increases faster the more decoherent a system is, resulting in runaway exponential growth. It is not a new phenomenon, and humans have always countered it through carefully finding ways to do more with less, unifying disparate patterns and models into a cohesive whole. However, the widespread use of AI is currently producing it at a rate that is unsustainable. A form of learned helplessness has emerged, along with a paradoxical false confidence, caused by the ways LLMs provide the illusion of work without actually forcing us to think through the details. This de-skilling of software engineers only shifts the balance of power even further away from developers - who can no longer raise the alarm. At its worst, AI turns tech workers into “meat proxies” who spend their days massaging prompts and letting Claude figure out if the work is actually complete. Systemic decay It’s not just programmers. It’s the whole chain, top to bottom. Everyone is using AI, especially in big tech. Claude generates code because the engineer wrote a prompt. The prompt comes from a ticket that was written with Claude. The project manager wrote the ticket based on a summary of a document, that was written by, and then summarised back, by Claude. The document uses statistics from a calculation, by Claude. The business is panicking about the stock market, and the stock market prioritises short term trends over long term engineering. Does this sound accurate? It’s a caricature, but not by a lot. I believe that tech companies risk losing their “organisational cognition” - their ability to think and respond as a coherent unit. This is the real threat: a scenario where nothing in the system is done with intent, and nobody in the system has control. We generate complexity faster than we can tame it. Look at the problems I’ve outlined. They are about systems of excessive complexity, made of parts that need to work perfectly or else everything falls apart. These parts are being individually corroded by corner-cutting, cost-cutting, overcomplication, over-reliance on uncompensated work and - I fear - helplessness amongst the people who build digital infrastructure. What is at stake? This is a threat to all of us. The tech industry is now critical to everyday life. It’s the software that controls your flights, your banking, your petrol pumps, your TV, your payroll. It’s what allows you to navigate roads and find your friends. It’s how you date and how you eat. It’s how you’re reading this. Society has extended trust, too much trust, into technical systems that are now demonstrating systemic deterioration. I do not think society, government, or institutions are prepared for a world where the incidents and outages of 2026 become commonplace. They too are extending the chain of dependencies, assumptions, complexity and unwarranted trust. Each layer, each link in the chain is a new point of attack that can subvert everything on top of it. The internet is at a breaking point. The software we build is not legible enough to bear the responsibility the world is giving it. We are telling ourselves the AI revolution is succeeding, precisely because of the rate at which we are generating complexity. The actual load-bearing parts of the ecosystem - open source, engineering-led judgement - are crumbling away. I think we are only at the beginning of a very painful phase. This is not a blip, and it’s not an aberration - it’s the new normal. Back to all posts © 2026 Jimmy Breck-McKye. Built with Astro.

title: Universal XSS in uBlock Origin from website-driven element picker
body_text: Universal XSS in uBlock Origin from website-driven element picker iter.ca â¢ About â¢ Uses â¢ Accounts â¢ Notes Universal XSS in uBlock Origin from website-driven element picker By Smitty van Bodegom (loops) Â· Nov 15, 2026 Earlier this month I found a one-click universal XSS issue with uBlock Origin (the MV2 Firefox version, although a similar but less problematic issue also affected the MV3 version, uBO Lite), where a malicious website could trick the extension into adding arbitrary trusted filters. Trusted filters can inject JavaScript code into pages, and so the malicious website could create a trusted filter on another website and run arbitrary JS in the context of any site. This issue is fixed now; you can read the GitHub advisory for some more details. GPT-5.6 Sol did most of the hard work of finding the issue. I figured there might be some kind of UXSS from filter injection, so I asked it to take a look, and it found the issue. I then checked and verified the issue it proposed. I wrote all of the prose in this post myself; Claude wrote most of the code for the PoC. The issue uBlock Origin has an element picker that you can pull up by right-clicking on the page. You can use this to create a filter rule to block an element on the page without leaving the page. The element picker is implemented by injecting an iframe to a URL like moz-extension://76b2331a-894c-4d25-8b89-fcce37e79cc4/web_accessible_resources/epicker-ui.html . That page can talk to the extension background script and tell it to add filters. Basically the attack here is: Figure out the element picker URL Create our own invisible (opacity 0) iframe that embeds it Drive the picker to put the filter we want in it Position the invisible iframe to trick the user into pressing the invisible “Create” button Figuring out the element picker URL On Firefox, the only information we needed to figure out was the extension internal UUID which is random per-installation. On the default setup uBO has a lootdest.*##+js(no-fetch-if, adsbygoogle, war:googlesyndication_adsbygoogle.js) filter rule (from uAssets), which hooks fetch . From inside the fetch hook, it makes an XHR request to moz-extension://<extension UUID>/web_accessible_resources/googlesyndication_adsbygoogle.js and returns the response from that as the fetch body, instead of actually making the request. The filter rule is intended to replace a network request for JS from an ad server with a dummy script that has the correct API but doesn’t do anything. But the attacker website can itself hook the XHR made from inside the no-fetch-if hook to extract the random extension UUID. const origOpen = XMLHttpRequest . prototype . open ; XMLHttpRequest . prototype . open = function ( m , url , ... a ) { const e = /^moz-extension:\/\/[^/]+/ . exec ( url ); if ( e ) { e [ 0 ] // <- has the extension UUID! } return origOpen . call ( this , m , url , ... a ); }; Then the attacker website can run fetch('/adsbygoogle.js').catch(() => {}); to trigger the filter, and make their hooked XHR run. Note that there are several ways that the extension internal UUID could be leaked; it’s not just this one filter rule. Creating an iframe Then you can use that to iframe the element picker. Given an iframe element in the page, you just set its src to `moz-extension://${origin}/web_accessible_resources/epicker-ui.html` . Sending messages to it Now we can drive the element picker. We can create a MessageChannel and do iframe.contentWindow.postMessage({ what: 'epickerStart' }, '*', [ch.port2]); to send it to the picker iframe. Then we talk to it: it sends us a start message, we send it a showDialog message with a filter and a resultsetDetails message 1 to enable the create button and set opt . Normally the picker restricts what filters you can enter, and doesn’t let you add scriptlet filters. But there’s a trick we can do to add arbitrary filters. There’s an opt field we set in the second message which is normally the type of network request to match (like image ), and gets appended to the filter with a $ if set, like $image . But since we control it, we can put a newline in it and make it "image\ngoogle.com##+js(trusted-rpnt, script, ...)" to inject an arbitrary trusted filter that injects a script. 2 This is where the main issue is - the element picker shouldn’t accept messages from the attacker. One of the fixes was having a secret password that the real element picker gets from the content script, that the element picker sends in the initial postMessage. Getting the click I didn’t bother actually implementing this, but malicious websites could overlay stuff on top of the embedded element picker or make it invisible by setting the iframe opacity to 0. So as long as the website can get the user to click on the page, it can add arbitrary trusted filters for arbitrary domains. Filters added by the element picker are always treated as trusted (at least until a recompile), which is why it can add a trusted filter. If the user later changes their custom filters it would cause a recompile, clearing the filter trust. But in practice the attacker could just immediately open the victim webpage, so this doesn’t help much. Originally I sent that message in reply to a dialogSetFilter message from the picker, but it turns out you can just send it right away instead of waiting to reply.  ↩︎ Assuming the shown filter is a network filter.  ↩︎ Related Bypassing the GitHub workflow permission with nested Git tags Malleating Git commit signatures Forging signed commits on GitHub Don't run your own mailserver Patching protobufs poetically X: @_smitop ð§ m e&#x000000000000000000000000000000040;it er.c a Discord: @moreloops Content license: CC-BY-SA 4.0 Tags: security programming Comments Subscribe to my occasional email newsletter:

Stuff About Steve Startup Tools Secret History Books for Startups Slides/Videos Raising Money What’s Next For Nvidia? Posted on November 15, 2026 by steve blank Nvidia’s board announced that Jensen Huang had resigned 33 years after he co-founded the company. What happens to a company when a visionary CEO is gone? Most often innovation dies and the company coasts for years on momentum and its brand. Rarely does it regain its former glory. That’s the danger facing Nvidia. Here’s what their board should be considering. Here’s why. Jensen Huang reinvented Nvidia three times. In 2006 he launched CUDA , turning a graphics chip for PC gamers into a general-purpose computing platform – and funded it for years ahead of any revenue. In 2012, when researchers used Nvidia chips to win the ImageNet contest , he pointed the company to deep learning. In 2020, with the acquisition of Mellanox , Nvidia went from selling boards with GPUs to selling integrated racks that power AI datacenters. These were not just product transitions, but radical business model transitions; new channels, new customers and new markets. Nvidia pivoted from a vendor of graphics boards, to a software platform, and then to systems company. It’s hard to imagine a CEO focused on executing an existing business model funding CUDA through those years. Steve Jobs did the same at Apple, transforming it from a niche computer company into the most profitable company in the world. Between 2001 and 2008, Jobs reinvented the company three times. Visionary CEOs are not “just” great at assuring world-class execution of a successful business model, they are also world-class innovators . The best are agile and know how to pivot, making substantive changes to their business model while or before their market has shifted. The very best of them shape markets – they know how to create new markets by seeing opportunities before anyone else . They remain entrepreneurs . Visionary CEOs don’t need someone else to demo the company’s key products for them. They deeply understand products, and they have their own coherent and consistent vision of where the industry/business models and customers are today, and where they need to take the company. They know who their customers are because they spend time talking to them. They use strategy committees and the exec staff for advice, but none of these CEOs pivot by committee . Microsoft and Apple are two examples of what happens when a visionary CEO is replaced by an execution CEO. Microsoft and the Cost of Missing the Next Market Microsoft entered the 21st century as the dominant software provider for anyone who interacted with a computing device. After running Microsoft for 25 years, Bill Gates handed the reins of Microsoft to Steve Ballmer in January 2000. Ballmer went on to run Microsoft for the next 14 years. Ballmer organized the company around execution of its then current strengths – Windows and Office businesses. He tripled Microsoft’s sales to $78 billion and profits more than doubled from $9 billion to $22 billion, but those results hid missed opportunities that would reshape computing. Ballmer failed to understand and execute on the five most important technology trends of the 21st century: in search – losing to Google; in smartphones – losing to Apple; in mobile operating systems – losing to Google/Apple; in media – losing to Apple/Netflix; and in the cloud – losing to Amazon. In early 2014, Satya Nadella took charge. Nadella got Microsoft organized around the cloud (Azure), freed the Office and Azure teams from Windows and killed the phone business. Nadella saved Microsoft from irrelevance. Today Microsoft is worth about $4 trillion . It is one of the few companies that regained its former glory, after its board replaced a salesman with a product and engineering insider. Innovation CEOs Hire Execution VPs Successful visionary CEOs build an executive staff of world-class operating executives and technical leaders (and they unconsciously force out any world-class innovators from their direct reports). The problem is in a company driven by a visionary CEO; there is only one visionary. Nvidia is the extreme case. Jensen had about 60 direct reports and discouraged one-on-one meetings. No long-term plans. Much like Jobs, he made himself the point where technical, product and business decisions came together. Replacing that role is harder than filling a box on an organization chart. He said he didn’t believe in succession planning . When visionary founders depart (resignation, death, firing, etc.), their operating executives believe it’s their turn to run the company. At Microsoft, Bill Gates chose Steve Ballmer, and at Apple Steve Jobs chose Tim Cook. Jensen anointed no one. Once in charge, one of the first things these operations/execution CEOs do is to get rid of the chaos and turbulence in the organization. Execution CEOs value stability, process and repeatable execution. On one hand that’s great for predictability, but it often starts a creative death spiral – creative people start to leave, and other executors (without the innovation talent of the old leader) are put into more senior roles – hiring more process people, which in turn forces out the remaining creative talent. This culture shift ripples down from the top and what once felt like a company on a mission to change the world now feels like another job . (Amazon is a counterexample. Before succeeding Jeff Bezos, Andy Jassy had already founded and led AWS . He was an innovator who had built a new business inside the existing company.) At Nvidia this step isn’t optional. No one else can run a company with 60 direct reports, so the next CEO’s first move will be to add layers of management. Why Tim Cook Was the New Steve Ballmer Tim Cook ran Apple for 15 years. Apple under Cook grew its revenues from $108 billion to $416 billion and its market value from $350 billion to about $4 trillion. The iPhone continued its annual upgrades of incremental improvements. The transition to Apple silicon showed that major technical change on the chip level was possible under his leadership. But Apple silicon was a better engine for the existing products Apple already had, not a new market. Apple stumbled badly on the one major product category launched under Cook – Apple Vision Pro and missed badly on AI (Siri was actually first with a Chatbot.) This year it turned to Google to help fix Siri. In September 2026 Cook handed the job to John Ternus. How Nvidia Could Miss the Boat The threat to Nvidia is already visible: its biggest customers are becoming its competitors. Google, Amazon, Microsoft, Meta, OpenAI and Tesla are all building their own AI chips . Jensen’s answer was to keep innovating and bring to market a new generation of chips every year, build a moat around an integrated hardware and software platform ( CUDA ), and invest ~$50 billion in the AI labs that run on Nvidia. It’s likely these are the bets an execution CEO trims first. The irony is that in the 21st century, the tighter you hold on to your current product/markets, the likelier you will be disrupted . The rapid change of technology will create new disruptions that will force “bet the company” decisions about product direction, markets, pricing, supply chain, operations and the reorganization necessary to execute a new business model. In the GPU market, the difference between market dominance and Chapter 11 may be a hands-on product/customer, and business model-centric CEO with an entrepreneurial vision of the future. Four Challenges for the Board of Directors The dilemma facing the board at Nvidia or any board of directors on the departure of an innovative CEO is strategic : Do we still want to be an innovative, risk taking company? Or should we now focus on execution of our core business, reduce our risky bets and maximize shareholder return. Ultimately a board would like both – preserving the speed and ambition of Jensen’s decision-making while distributing enough authority for the company to function without him. Tactically , that question results in asking: Do you search for another innovator from outside, promote one of the executors or go deeper down the organization to find an innovator? Herein lies four challenges. Steve Jobs and Bill Gates chose execution executives as their successors. The result was they confused world-class execution with the passion for product and customers, and market insight. From the perspective of Gates there was no difference between him and Ballmer and Jobs believed Cook could be equally creative. Yet history has shown they were world-class stewards of a business model each had been handed. Yet long-term survival in markets that change rapidly require innovation and execution.. Nvidia’s board has a different version of this problem. Jensen suggested no one, and he left the board the day he left the job. The decision belongs to a board in crisis, led by the first chair the company has ever had. Boards in crisis reach for stability. That gets you an execution CEO by a different road. Nvidia’s board should ask what its candidates have built under uncertainty. If the board decides that the company needs another innovator at the helm, you can almost guarantee that the best executor – the number 2 and/or 3 vice president in the company – will leave, feeling that they deserved the job. Now the board is faced with not only having lost its CEO, but potentially the best of the executive staff. Many innovative/visionary CEOs have become part of the company’s brand. Steve Jobs, Mark Zuckerberg, Elon Musk and Jensen Huang. This isn’t a new phenomenon, think of 20th-century icons like Walt Disney, Edwin Land at Polaroid and Henry Ford. But they’re not only an external face to the company, they were often the touchstone for internal decision-making. Years after a visionary CEO is gone, companies are still asking, “What would Walt Disney/Steve Jobs/Henry Ford have done?” rather than figuring out what they should now be doing in the changing market. Jensen was more than the brand. He set Nvidia’s foreign policy, and was the company’s face in Washington, Beijing and Taipei. No Nvidia operating VP has done that job. The next Nvidia CEO inherits a Congress and investigators asking how many restricted Nvidia chips reached China. As companies grow larger and management falls prey to the fallacy that it only exists to maximize shareholder short-term return on investment, companies become risk averse. Large companies and their boards live in fear of losing what they spent years gaining (customers, market share, revenue, profits.) This may work in stable markets and technologies. But today very few of those remain. And certainly not Nvidia’s market. Lessons Learned Nvidia’s order book and CUDA will make the next two or three years look fine no matter who is CEO (unless a meaningful share of that revenue turns out to be chips that were diverted to China .) Innovation CEOs are almost always replaced by one of their execution VPs If they have inherited a powerful business model (like Nvidia) this often results in gains in revenue and profits that can continue for years However, as soon as the market, business model, technology shifts, these execution CEOs are ill-equipped to deal with the change The result is a company obsoleted by more agile competitors and their company is left to live off momentum in its twilight years Nvidia’s board has to decide what it is hiring its next CEO to do. Executing today’s business is essential. So is reinventing it before someone else makes it obsolete. body_text: Old Bitly links hijacked in Burger King, McDonald’s and Trump tweets | Ransomnews Close Menu Home News Security Privacy Cybercrime Threat Groups Ransomware Explainers Stealer Logs AI OSINT Tools Ransomtracker Ransomware attacks today Stealercheck FortiBleed Checker Site Check Data Ransomware statistics Ransom payment rate Breach verification Infostealer statistics Newsletter About Us Facebook X (Twitter) Instagram Threads Ransomnews Home News Security Privacy Cybercrime Threat Groups Ransomware Explainers Stealer Logs AI OSINT Tools Ransomtracker Ransomware attacks today Stealercheck FortiBleed Checker Site Check Data Ransomware statistics Ransom payment rate Breach verification Infostealer statistics Newsletter About Us Facebook X (Twitter) LinkedIn Ransomnews Security Old Bitly links hijacked in Burger King, McDonald’s and Trump tweets By Ransomnews Research Team November 15, 2026 Updated: November 15, 2026 No Comments 21 Mins Read 26,626 Views Share Facebook Twitter Pinterest LinkedIn Tumblr Email Copy Link Share Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Email Copy Link Update, 15 November, 23:40 UTC: CNN reports redirected Bitly links in old posts from Bill Gates, Justin Trudeau, Mike Pence, the FBI and the US Department of Defense as well. Our third check of the Trump links, at 23:35 UTC, found nothing new: 49 links re-created years after their tweets still work. Update, 15 November, 22:30 UTC: Bitly has confirmed the problem. In a post on X at 19:13 UTC it said it had identified an issue that “allowed bad actors to repurpose certain old, inactive links” and send people to unrelated content. Bitly said it has suspended the accounts involved and is disabling the affected links. It added that its Trust and Safety team is working on protections against similar misuse. Earlier today, we identified an issue that allowed bad actors to repurpose certain old, inactive links to redirect people to content unrelated to the original posts. We have suspended the accounts involved and are disabling the affected links. Our Trust and Safety team is working… — Bitly (@Bitly) November 15, 2026 Update, 15 November, 19:30 UTC: The Burger King and McDonald’s links no longer redirect. Both were still working at 15:05 UTC and returned Bitly’s “Link Deactivated” page by 19:22 UTC. The same has happened to the two extra Trump links we verified and to six of the seven links in our sample that pointed somewhere new. The seventh now shows a Bitly warning that the account that created it has been suspended. The 49 re-created links that look like the originals still work. Burger King’s X account was not hacked. A Bitly short link in a tweet the chain posted on 24 July 2011 was registered again by someone else on 15 November 2026 and pointed at Wikipedia’s list of Nazi concentration camps. The tweet was advertising a restaurant locator. A post quoting it passed 2 million views within hours, and Burger King’s original has since become unavailable. It was not the only one. Eighteen minutes earlier a Bitly link in a McDonald’s tweet from 7 June 2011 was registered the same way and pointed at Wikipedia’s article on the September 11 attacks. Ransomnews also checked 97 Bitly links in Donald Trump’s tweets from 2009 to 2013, taken from a public archive. Bitly’s own link pages show that 56 were created after the tweets they sit in, and a 57th is blocked by Bitly as malicious or spam. Four were registered on 15 November. Two more, created in January 2024 and January 2025, point at domains that copy the names of crypto services. In brief Burger King posted the tweet on 24 July 2011 with the short link bit[.]ly/19BFiM. Bitly’s information page for that link gives a creation time of 05:32 UTC on 15 November 2026 and a destination on Wikipedia. A link in a McDonald’s tweet from 7 June 2011, bit[.]ly/mLWJO0, was created again at 05:14 UTC the same morning, 18 minutes before Burger King’s. It opens Wikipedia’s article on the September 11 attacks. Both tweets have since become unavailable. Nobody posted from either company’s account. The links changed hands on Bitly’s side, so the old tweets send readers wherever the new owners choose. Of 97 Bitly links in Donald Trump’s tweets from 2009 to 2013, 40 are still the original. Another 49 were created again later but lead where the tweets suggest, 48 of them in a 17-minute run on 26 May 2023. Seven lead somewhere else and one is blocked by Bitly. Four of those seven were registered on 15 November 2026 between 07:49 and 09:57 UTC. They open a Roblox profile, a YouTube video (twice) and a Wikipedia article about Trump and Jeffrey Epstein. One Trump tweet from April 2011 carries three links to videos of his children. All three have been replaced. Bitly’s help pages say the ending of a bit.ly link cannot be reused, even after the account behind it is deleted. In February 2025 it was reported to have fixed a bug that allowed this. We found no public statement from Bitly, Burger King or McDonald’s by 14:30 UTC on 15 November. By 19:22 UTC both links returned Bitly’s “Link Deactivated” page. None of the seven Trump links that pointed somewhere new redirects any more. Bitly confirmed the issue on X at 19:13 UTC. It said it has suspended the accounts involved and is disabling the affected links. CNN reported the same evening that old posts from Bill Gates, Justin Trudeau, Mike Pence, the FBI and the US Department of Defense were affected too. We have not checked those links ourselves. Was Burger King hacked? No. Nothing was posted from Burger King’s account and nothing suggests anyone got into it. The tweet is 15 years old and reads as it always did, pointing followers to “our handy restaurant locator” through a Bitly link. What changed is where that link goes. As with the Microsoft 365 outage three days earlier, the first question people asked was whether it was an attack on the company, and the answer is the same. Bitly keeps a public information page for every short link. Add a plus sign to the end of the address and it shows where the link points and when it was created. For bit[.]ly/19BFiM that page gives the destination as Wikipedia’s “List of Nazi concentration camps” and the creation time as 15 November 2026, 05:32 UTC. A link printed in a tweet from 2011 can only carry a 2026 creation date if the same ending was issued a second time. We tested the method on links nobody disputes. A link whose creator says he made it in 2009 shows a 2009 creation date. A custom link tweeted by a YouTube channel on 21 June 2017 shows 20 June 2017. Among the Trump links that are still original, 32 of 40 were created on the day of the tweet or the day before. Burger King’s 2011 tweet as it appeared on the morning of 15 November 2026, quoted by another user. Screenshot: X. The post that spread it came from an X user at 06:51 UTC, 79 minutes after the link was created, and had 2.2 million views by early afternoon. OH LORD https://t.co/QlferLVmNL pic.twitter.com/sk6ceitzXd — The Wizard 🐧 (@42069volshebnik) November 15, 2026 By 13:45 UTC the Burger King post inside it was showing as unavailable. We do not know whether Burger King removed it or X did. The short link was still redirecting to Wikipedia at 13:47 UTC. Was McDonald’s hacked? No. Its link was changed 18 minutes before Burger King’s. On 7 June 2011 McDonald’s tweeted a Bitly link to something its team in Sweden had done. Bitly’s information page for bit[.]ly/mLWJO0 shows the link was created at 05:14 UTC on 15 November 2026, and it redirects to Wikipedia’s article on the September 11 attacks. The tweet was returning a not-found error when we checked at 14:20 UTC. The two changes are close in time and alike in style. The X user Alex Greenland, who spotted both timestamps, thinks one person or group is probably behind them. Nothing we have seen proves that. This Burger King Bitly link was changed at 05:32 UK time today (15 Nov 2026), which is very close to the change of McDonald's tweet Bitly link at 05:14 today. This means it is likely the same actor or group of actors is making these changes. https://t.co/2gqoms5veu pic.twitter.com/u4OxXaPkn2 — Alex Greenland (@ajrgd) November 15, 2026 How does an old Bitly link get hijacked? Someone registers its ending again. The part of a Bitly link after the slash is called the back-half. Bitly generates one at random, or the user types a custom one. If an old link stops existing and its back-half can be claimed, whoever claims it decides where every tweet, email, PDF and printed QR code carrying that link now leads. No password is stolen and no account is touched, so the brand that posted the link sees nothing wrong. Bitly says this cannot happen. Its help page on deleted accounts states that bit.ly links keep working and that their back-halves “cannot be re-used”, whether they were generated or custom. A separate page says Bitly deletes accounts that have been inactive for three years. The creation dates we collected do not fit the first statement. Back-halves that appear in tweets from 2009 to 2012 belong to links created between 2023 and today. It has happened before. In February 2025 Disruptionist reported that memecoin promoters had taken over Bitly links in 2013 posts by Donald Trump and Melania Trump and pointed them at token listings. According to that report, a bug let people claim a back-half once the original link or its account had been deleted or deactivated, and Bitly fixed it and switched off the hijacked links. Links created on 15 November 2026 show the same thing is possible now. The X user Damin Toell identified it as link hijacking at 07:25 UTC and noted that old Trump posts were affected too. Someone is hijacking old bitly links. A lot of this going on with old Trump posts, too. https://t.co/BB5c5BnlFV pic.twitter.com/7JiBxWbirZ — Damin Toell (@damintoell) November 15, 2026 At 09:18 UTC another user described the method in a post that has been viewed more than 46,000 times. Three more Trump links were registered in the 40 minutes that followed. Free tool How does your own site score? Run the same forty passive checks against your own domain: TLS and certificates, security headers, SPF and DMARC, cookies before consent, and what your stack quietly reveals. A grade out of 100 in about fifteen seconds. Your domain Check site No signup. Nothing installed. We only request what your site already serves publicly. How many old links have been replaced? More than half of the ones we tested. We took every tweet Donald Trump’s account posted from 2009 to 2016 from the Trump Twitter Archive data set on GitHub, left out retweets and extracted the bit.ly links. That gave 97 different links, first used between 2009 and 2013, with 61 of them from 2011. We chose this account because its old posts were named in the reports of 15 November and in the 2025 case, and because a full public archive exists. For each link we recorded where it redirects and the creation date on Bitly’s information page, at about 13:45 UTC on 15 November 2026. 57 of 97 Bitly links in old Trump tweets are no longer the original Bitly links in @realDonaldTrump tweets from 2009 to 2013, by what the link is today. Checked on 15 November 2026. Created again, leads where the tweet suggests 49 Still the original link 40 Created again, leads somewhere else 7 Blocked by Bitly 1 Source: Ransomnews check of Bitly link information pages. Tweets from the Trump Twitter Archive data set. Forty links are untouched. Forty-nine were created again later and lead to addresses that fit the tweets: mostly videos on Trump’s YouTube channel, plus pages at CNBC, CNN and the Wall Street Journal. Forty-eight of those were created between 14:55 and 15:12 UTC on 26 May 2023, roughly one every 20 seconds. We do not know who did that. It looks like a repair job by someone who knew where each link used to go, and it means those back-halves were free to claim by May 2023. That leaves eight links that now lead somewhere their tweets never pointed. Tweet date What the tweet promoted Link created again Where it goes now 3 Jun 2009 An iGoogle page 15 Nov 2026, 07:49 UTC A Roblox user profile 1 Jul 2010 A golf course in Scotland 15 Nov 2026, 09:36 UTC A YouTube video 17 Sep 2010 A QVC jewellery show 15 Nov 2026, 09:47 UTC The same YouTube video 7 Oct 2010 A golf course in Scotland 15 Nov 2026, 09:57 UTC Wikipedia’s article on Trump and Jeffrey Epstein 14 Mar 2011 A video blog 29 Jan 2025, 21:09 UTC test[.]com 25 Apr 2011 A video of Donald Trump Jr. 18 Jan 2025, 21:43 UTC worldlibertyfinancial-ai[.]com 25 Apr 2011 A video of Eric Trump 17 Jan 2024, 11:08 UTC dappradars[.]website 25 Apr 2011 A video of Ivanka Trump Not shown Blocked by Bitly as malicious or spam Creation times are from Bitly’s information pages, read on 15 November 2026. Domains are written with brackets so they cannot be clicked. One tweet, three replaced links On 25 April 2011 the account posted three Bitly links to “The Next Generation” videos of Donald Trump Jr., Ivanka Trump and Eric Trump. The first now leads to worldlibertyfinancial-ai[.]com, a domain that borrows the name of World Liberty Financial, the Trump family’s crypto venture. The third leads to dappradars[.]website, one letter away from the crypto analytics site DappRadar, at a path named “eligibility/check”. Bitly blocks the second with a notice that it was “flagged as redirecting to malicious or spam content”. WHOIS records from WhoisXML API show both domains were registered afresh after the links were created. The current registration of dappradars[.]website began at 02:56 UTC on 15 November 2026, through Hostinger, although the Bitly link that points there was created in January 2024. The domain now forwards to a YouTube video. The current registration of worldlibertyfinancial-ai[.]com dates from 11 April 2026, through Namecheap, almost 15 months after the link was created, and its HTTPS certificate failed verification when we checked. We have not seen what either domain served when the links were first made. A replaced link can be replaced again. When the domain behind it lapses, the next buyer inherits whatever traffic the old tweet still sends. More Trump links outside our 97 X users found replaced Bitly links in Trump tweets from 2012 and 2013 that the archive stores only as t.co addresses. We checked two. The link in a tweet of 10 January 2013 was created at 23:52 UTC on 14 November 2026 and opens a page on Steam. The link in a tweet of 10 September 2012 was created at 01:04 UTC on 15 November and opens a YouTube video. Late on 14 November is the earliest change in this wave that we have seen. Which re-created links still work? We ran the same check on the 97 Trump links twice more, at 19:25 and 23:35 UTC on 15 November. The seven links that pointed somewhere new no longer redirect. The other 49 links created years after their tweets still do: 48 were made within 17 minutes of each other on 26 May 2023 and one in February 2025. They point to what look like the original pages, mostly YouTube videos and news articles. We do not know who re-created them or why. The 40 original links work as before. How we counted We used the archive’s condensed yearly files for 2009 to 2016 and found bit.ly links only in tweets up to 2013. From late 2011 Twitter wrapped links in its own t.co shortener, and the archive stores most later links in that form (1,218 of them in 2012), so Bitly links behind those are not among our 97. A link counts as created again when Bitly’s information page shows a creation date more than 30 days after the first tweet that used it. In practice the gap was at least 11 years in every case. Destinations were read from the redirect header without opening the pages. The count covers one account and one link shortener. It shows that these links were claimed. How many of Bitly’s older links can be claimed is something only Bitly can answer. Domain registration data is from WhoisXML API. Who else was affected? CNN reported on the evening of 15 November that old posts from Bill Gates, Justin Trudeau, Mike Pence, the FBI and the US Department of Defense carried redirected Bitly links too, along with a 2013 post from McDonald’s Indonesia account. It counted at least a dozen in Trump’s posts, in a wave that appears limited to posts from 2009 to 2014. Burger King told CNN it had nothing to do with the redirects. We have not checked those links ourselves. Bitly was already disabling affected links when they were reported, and a disabled link no longer shows when it was created. The accounts we verified directly are Burger King, McDonald’s and Donald Trump. What happened on 15 November 2026? The first change we found came late on 14 November. The McDonald’s and Burger King links followed at 05:14 and 05:32 UTC the next morning. All times below are UTC and on 15 November unless stated. How the Bitly link hijacking unfolded Saturday 14 to Sunday 15 November 2026. All times are UTC. Links and domains registered by someone else Posts, statements and our checks 00:00 06:00 12:00 18:00 00:00 Saturday 14 November: the earliest change we found 23:52 Link taken A link in a 2013 Trump tweet is registered and pointed at a page on Steam, the earliest change we found. Sunday 15 November, morning: the brand links are taken 01:04 Link taken A link in a 2012 Trump tweet is registered and pointed at a YouTube video. 02:56 Domain dappradars[.]website, the target of a Trump link replaced in 2024, is registered afresh. 05:14 Link taken The back-half in McDonald’s 2011 tweet is registered and pointed at Wikipedia. 05:32 Link taken The back-half in Burger King’s 2011 tweet is registered and pointed at Wikipedia. 06:51 X An X user quotes the Burger King tweet. The post goes on to pass 2 million views. 07:25 X Another user identifies it as link hijacking and says old Trump posts are affected. 07:49 Link taken A link in a 2009 Trump tweet is registered and pointed at a Roblox profile. 09:18 X A user describes the method in public. 09:36 to 09:57 Links taken Three links in 2010 Trump tweets are registered. Sunday 15 November, afternoon and evening: Bitly responds 13:45 Burger King Burger King’s post shows as unavailable. Its link still redirects to Wikipedia. 14:20 McDonald’s McDonald’s post returns a not-found error. Its link still redirects to Wikipedia too. 15:05 Our check Both links still redirect to Wikipedia. 19:13 Bitly Bitly says on X that an issue let old, inactive links be repurposed, that it has suspended the accounts involved and that it is disabling the affected links. Why it matters: this is the first confirmation from Bitly that old links could be taken over. 19:22 Our check Both links return Bitly’s “Link Deactivated” page. So do six of the seven Trump links in our sample that pointed somewhere new and the two we verified outside it. The seventh shows a warning that the account that created it has been suspended. 21:10 CNN CNN reports redirected links in old posts from Bill Gates, Justin Trudeau, Mike Pence, the FBI and the US Department of Defense. 23:35 Our check Our third check finds no further change. Forty-nine re-created links in the Trump sample still redirect. Status Now The Burger King and McDonald’s links no longer redirect, and neither do the Trump links that pointed somewhere new. Forty-nine re-created links in the Trump sample still work. Bitly has not said how many links were taken. Checked at 23:35 UTC on 15 November. Link creation times are from Bitly’s information pages and post times are from X. Checks are our own. CNN’s report is timed by its publication. Last checked 23:35 UTC, 15 November 2026. Why does a joke link matter? Because the same move works for fraud. The examples from 15 November are pranks: a Wikipedia page, a game profile, a video. The 2025 wave pushed memecoins, and two of the Trump links in our table lead to domains named after crypto services. A link inside an old post from a verified brand, a bank, a ministry or a news outlet carries that account’s credibility, and X shows the post exactly as it was written. Readers have no reason to doubt it. The exposure is wider than X. The same short links sit in old emails, PDFs, slide decks, printed QR codes and help pages. Security researchers file this under broken link hijacking : a link outlives the thing it pointed to, and someone else moves in. What should brands and readers do? Any organisation that posted short links years ago should assume some of them are no longer its own. List the short links in your old posts. Export your post archive from each platform and pull out every bit.ly address. Check each one. Add a plus sign to the link and compare Bitly’s creation date with the date of your post. A later date means the link is no longer yours. Remove what you cannot fix. Delete posts whose links were replaced or no longer resolve, and report replaced links to Bitly. Use a short domain you own for new links , so nobody else can issue the same address. For everyone else, the checks take a few seconds. Do not trust a link because the post is old or the account is verified. The account owner may have no control over where it goes. Preview before you click. Adding a plus sign to a bit.ly link shows the destination without visiting it. Be most careful with pages that ask you to sign in or connect a crypto wallet. What happens next? Bitly has to say whether old back-halves can still be claimed and what it will do about the ones already taken. We found no public statement from Bitly, Burger King or McDonald’s by 14:30 UTC on 15 November. Later that day the links that pointed somewhere new were deactivated, and 49 others created years after their tweets were left working. Bitly confirmed the issue on X at 19:13 UTC and said it was still disabling affected links. Its statement does not say how many links were taken or how. Checks like this one are what our breach verification desk is for, and we will update this article when either company responds or the numbers move. Frequently asked questions Was Burger King hacked in November 2026? No. Nothing was posted from Burger King’s X account. A Bitly short link in a tweet from 24 July 2011 was registered again by someone else on 15 November 2026, so the old tweet began sending readers to a different page. Was McDonald’s hacked? No. A Bitly link in a McDonald’s tweet from 7 June 2011 was registered again at 05:14 UTC on 15 November 2026 and pointed at Wikipedia’s article on the September 11 attacks. Nothing was posted from the McDonald’s account. Why did a Burger King tweet link to a list of Nazi concentration camps? The tweet’s Bitly link, bit[.]ly/19BFiM, originally advertised a restaurant locator. Bitly’s information page shows the link was created again at 05:32 UTC on 15 November 2026 with a Wikipedia article as its destination. Burger King did not choose that destination. What is Bitly link hijacking? It is when someone registers the ending of an old Bitly link that no longer exists and points it at a page of their choice. Every old post, email or document that carries the link then leads to the new destination. No account is broken into. How can I tell whether a Bitly link has been replaced? Add a plus sign to the end of the link. Bitly shows the destination and the date the link was created. If the creation date is later than the post or document the link appears in, the link is not the original. Were Donald Trump’s old tweets hacked? No. Ransomnews checked 97 Bitly links in tweets from 2009 to 2013. Fifty-six were created again after the tweets were posted and one is blocked by Bitly. Seven of them lead to destinations unrelated to the tweets, including two domains that copy the names of crypto services. Has Bitly fixed the problem? A fix was reported in February 2025 after links in Trump posts were pointed at memecoin pages. Links created on 15 November 2026 show that old endings can be claimed now. Bitly had made no public statement that we could find by 14:30 UTC that day. It confirmed the issue on X at 19:13 UTC and said it was disabling the affected links. It added that its Trust and Safety team is working on protections against similar misuse. Who else was affected by the Bitly link hijacking? CNN reported redirected Bitly links in old posts from Bill Gates, Justin Trudeau, Mike Pence, the FBI and the US Department of Defense, as well as Burger King, McDonald’s and Donald Trump. Ransomnews verified the Burger King, McDonald’s and Trump links directly. Are the hijacked Bitly links still active? The ones we tracked are not. By 19:22 UTC on 15 November 2026 the Burger King and McDonald’s links, and the Trump links that pointed somewhere new, returned Bitly’s “Link Deactivated” page. Bitly said it was still disabling affected links, so check any old short link before you trust it. title: Microsoft 365 outage leads to chlorine gas poisoning of 15 hotel guests
body_text: Phantasialand: Chlorunfall nach Microsoft-Panne zum Inhalt zur Navigation zur Suche Wetter Verkehr Menü öffnen Menü schließen Suche einblenden Suche ausblenden Eingabe löschen Suchen Mein NRW Übersicht Mein NRW Aachen und Eifel Bergisches Land Münsterland Niederrhein Ostwestfalen-Lippe Rheinland Ruhrgebiet Sauer- und Siegerland Politik Wirtschaft Sport Freizeit Kultur Wetter Verkehr ARD Mediathek ARD Sounds Hier findest du uns auch Mein NRW Übersicht Mein NRW Aachen und Eifel Bergisches Land Münsterland Niederrhein Ostwestfalen-Lippe Rheinland Ruhrgebiet Sauer- und Siegerland Politik Wirtschaft Sport Freizeit Kultur Wetter Verkehr ARD Mediathek ARD Sounds Suche einblenden Suche ausblenden Eingabe löschen Suchen Sie befinden sich hier: WDR Mein NRW Rheinland Rhein-Erft-Kreis Video starten, abbrechen mit Escape IT-Panne Schuld für Chlorgasunfall im Phantasialand | WDR aktuell Bildquelle: WDR WDR . 46 Sek. . Verfügbar bis 15.11.2028 . Nach IT-Störung bei Microsoft : 15 Gäste verletzt nach Chlorunfall im Phantasialand Stand: 16.11.2026, 19:15 Uhr Wegen der Microsoft-Störung am Freitag bekam das Phantasialand nicht mit, dass zu viel Chlor im Pool war. 15 Gäste wurden verletzt. Ein Cybersecurity-Architekt sieht den Fehler beim Freizeitpark, nicht bei Microsoft. Von Caroline Jüngermann , Friederike Müllender , Lara Burghardt und Martin Heuchel Diesem Problem waren wir alle ausgesetzt: Am Freitag gab es eine Störung, die den US-Softwarekonzern Microsoft lahmgelegt hat. Unter anderem das E-Mail-Programm Outlook. Betroffen war auch das Phantasialand. Durch die Störung kamen keine Mails an, wie das Unternehmen dem WDR am Samstag mitteilte. So bekam niemand mit, dass das Wartungssicherheitssystem der Saunalandschaft längst per Mail Alarm geschlagen hat. Denn das automatischen Dosiersystem hatte zu viel Chlor in den Pool gepumpt. Reizungen der Atemwege Dadurch wurden Gäste im Hotel Ling Bao des Phantasialands in Brühl verletzt. Sie haben über gesundheitliche Probleme geklagt, nachdem sie den Pool besucht hatten. Der wurde zeitweise gesperrt, konnte inzwischen aber wieder freigegeben werden, wie die Feuerwehr am Samstag dem WDR mitteilte. Wegen der Beschwerden der Hotel-Besucher wurden Rettungskräfte und die Feuerwehr gerufen. 13 Gäste klagten über Reizungen der Atemwege, letztlich stieg die Zahl der Betroffenen auf insgesamt 15. Überhöhter Chlorgehalt: Eine Person bleibt im Krankenhaus Zunächst hieß es, dass fünf Gäste ins Krankenhaus gebracht wurden, später wurde die Zahl auf vier korrigiert, eine Person davon blieb wegen einer mittelschweren Verletzung zur Beobachtung im Krankenhaus. Im Hotel ergaben Tests der Einsatzkräfte einen Defekt des automatischen Dosiersystems für den Pool. Dies hatte zu einem deutlich überhöhten Chlorgehalt geführt. Das Wasser wurde daher ausgetauscht. Betreiber der Mauritius-Therme wird hellhörig Die Nachricht über den Chlorunfall im Hotel im Phantasialand hat auch Max Wiesen, den Betreiber von "Mauritius Hotel und Therme", hellhörig werden lassen. "Da denkt man natürlich immer selber: Oh je, kann uns das auch passieren?" Max Wiesen, Betreiber von "Mauritius Hotel und Therme" Betreiber Max Wiese und Haustechniker Ingo Braun. Bildquelle: WDR/Friederike Müllender Das Erste was er dann gemacht habe, sei, mit seiner Technik zu sprechen, " wie wir da abgesichert sind. " Ansprechpartner für ihn ist sein Kollege Ingo Braun. Er ist bereits seit 15 Jahren Haustechniker und kennt sich mit den Pools aus. Der Wasserwert werde dreimal am Tag gemessen, sagt Braun. " Und wir haben ein Alarmsystem. Wenn in einem Pool etwas passiert, eine Überchlorung oder eine Unterchlorung, dann geht eine rote Lampe an, dass jeder Bescheid weiß. " Cybersecurity-Architekt sieht Fehler bei Phantasialand Auch Cybersecurity-Architekt und Informatiker Stephan Skrobisch hat den Fall im Phantasialand verfolgt, für ihn ist die Firma Microsoft nicht für den Vorfall verantwortlich. " Es ist ganz klar die Einrichtung der Anlage. Es wurde versäumt, einen weiteren Meldemechanismus zu implementieren ". Das könnte zum Beispiel ein akustisches Signal sein. title: Protomaps: Self-hosting map tiles has gotten cheap and easy
body_text: Protomaps: Self-hosting map tiles has gotten cheap and easy â Bruce RÃ¶ttgers Bruce RÃ¶ttgers about // portfolio // blog blog // dev // projects Protomaps: Self-hosting map tiles has gotten cheap and easy PMTiles is a tile format which works via HTTP Range requests and can be deployed as a single file to a storage bucket. 2026-11-15 // 4 min read // contents 1 Getting some Maps 2 Deploying to Bunny.net 3 Embedding the Map Â· Notes // contents 1 Getting some Maps 2 Deploying to Bunny.net 3 Embedding the Map Â· Notes I came across Protomaps in research for my latest project, Mapboard . 1 For most non-commercial projects, commercial APIs become prohibitively expensive if you ever go viral (Mapbox, for instance, charges $5 per 1k map loads once youâve exhausted the free tier). PMTiles, part of the Protomaps ecosystem, is a tile format that ships in a single file, accessible via Range requests, and is thus extremely portable and easy to deploy. For CDNs that support caching Range requests of large files, it requires no effort besides down- and uploading it to storage. For others, like Cloudflare, you can utilize an edge function to translate between the traditional x/y/z URL path and Range requests. Getting some Maps If all you want is the world map, getting it is as simple as going to the build page and downloading the latest daily build. However, more fun can be had with the CLI . For example, you can extract data for only a bounding box or specific zoom levels, to get a significantly smaller file. Deploying to Bunny.net One great CDN for deploying this is Bunny.net (affiliate link) . They support HTTP Range requests, donât collect personal data by default, 2 are headquartered in the EU, and offer low-cost access to a global network of CDN and edge storage servers. Pricing varies based on region and replication factor of the edge storage. But generally you pay $0.01/GB ($0.005/GB on the smaller Volume network) for bandwidth to Europe and North America, and $0.01/GB/month (no replication) to $0.055/GB/month (maximum replication) for storage. A high degree of replication mostly matters for latency in case of a cache miss (as the data is further replicated when itâs cached at the CDN PoPs). In practical terms, storing the 139GB world map with replication to most continents (5x) will run you about $5/month in storage fees. Loading a map of Europe on a laptop and zooming in on a city causes about 5MB of data to be transmitted, which would be $0.00005 â further navigations and reloads will be less expensive as more of the map gets cached locally. At $0.05/1k map loads that could be 100x cheaper than Mapbox. However, the actual bandwidth of course varies (less for people that bounce immediately, possibly tens of MB for heavy users). For Mapbox you only pay a flat fee per visit. Uploading the file Itâs a good idea to create a storage zone with S3 compatibility enabled, as uploading via the HTTP API timed out after 15 minutes for me. Then, with rclone installed, you can download and stream the file to the Bunny storage zone. Preferably in tmux or from a temporary VPS, if your connection isnât great. rclone config create bunnycdn s3 \ provider=Other \ access_key_id="<zone-name>" \ secret_access_key="<storage-key>" \ endpoint="https://<primary-region>-s3.storage.bunnycdn.com" rclone copyurl "<build-url>" "bunnycdn:<zone-name>/<filename>.pmtiles" \ --s3-chunk-size 256M \ --progress Configuring the pull zone Theoretically, at this point you just need to create a pull zone, select the storage zone as an origin, and youâre done. Practically, it would be sensible to change some settings. Allowed CORS origins can be configured under Security > General > Allowed referrers, so that other websites cannot embed your tiles. Youâll also want to verify under Caching that âOptimize for large object deliveryâ is enabled, as this makes it possible to cache Range requests. You might also want to dissuade people from downloading the whole file and leaving you with a large CDN bill. The most practical way Iâve found for this is limiting the download speed to 10kB/s after 10MB transmitted in a single request (using the âDownload speed limitsâ and âLimit afterâ settings under âNetwork limitsâ). Regular usage should never reach this amount. You may further want to introduce a requests/second limit (do note that legitimate usage can also quickly reach high numbers here) or a monthly bandwidth limit for the pull zone. Embedding the Map With the tiles deployed, the only thing left to do is to embed them in your website via MapLibre GL, for example. To do this, youâll need to install the pmtiles npm package and add the protocol and a style to MapLibre as detailed in the official installation guide . Congratulations, you now host your own cost-effective and highly available map of the world! // notes (2) Basically, Excalidraw but on a map for travel planning. Launch post coming soon. â The last octet of IP addresses is dropped. If you transmit personal data via the CDN, that is of course still processed. â // newsletter Stay updated on new blog posts and projects by me; sent less than once per week. subscribe â // written by Hi, Iâm Bruce, a Computer Science student at ETH Zurich. I build mobile apps, websites and other products, and I write about the interesting things I run into along the way. More about me â github // email // rss // letters reply by email â Please send an email if you wish to comment on this post. I will share select replies here with the author's permission. title: Tor Project Issues Rapid-Response DoS-Defense Fix Amid Sustained DDoS Attack

Stable Today, we are releasing 0.4.9.17 , which includes a series of security fixes. One fix in particular is especially important for relay DoS defenses related to IPv6 handling. This release comes in rapid response to the ongoing DDoS attack on the network, which has affected most relay operators. This is not an easy problem to address, as relays across the network are being overwhelmed by a massive flood of client circuits. We are actively evaluating additional defenses and so expect further releases in the near future. We want to extend a huge thank you to all relay operators who have been helping us deal with this ongoing attack. The tor-relays@ mailing list has been very active and we are very grateful for your time, effort, and support. Please, continue doing so! If you run a relay, please upgrade as soon as possible. No action item is required after upgrading. Thank you to all… except our attacker(s).
