Project Zero will disclose vulnerabilities 90 days after reporting
body_text: Policy and Disclosure: 2026 Edition - Project Zero Project Zero blog archive bug reports about Working at PZ 0day: spreadsheet 0day: Root Cause Analyses vulnerability disclosure policy reporting transparency search Policy and Disclosure: 2026 Edition 2026-Nov-13 Natalie Silvanovich Since 2021, Project Zero has followed a â90 + 30â vulnerability disclosure policy, allowing vendors up to 90 days to remediate a vulnerability plus an extra 30 days âsoak timeâ for patch rollout. Our goal was to encourage faster patching and give vendors time to deliver patches to users. The advent of AI-assisted vulnerability discovery and exploitation has changed the threat landscape such that the vulnerability remediation timeline encouraged by our disclosure policy is clearly insufficient. LLMs have increased the speed at which attackers can find and exploit vulnerabilities, alongside the risk that multiple parties, including malicious ones, discover the same bug. A vulnerability reported today presents a much higher immediate risk to users than one reported last year. In this new environment, it is crucial that vendors move towards remediating vulnerabilities faster. LLMs have also decreased the time it takes for attackers to reverse engineer and exploit a vulnerability based on a patch, to the extent that zero patch-to-exploitation time is a reasonable, though imperfect, model of attacker behavior. Patch soak time is no longer meaningful in a world where attackers can almost immediately determine bug details from a patch, and can put users at risk by creating a false sense of secrecy. âPatch gapâ is the time between a fix being released for a security vulnerability and the user installing the relevant update. It is equally crucial that vendors reduce patch gap, either by reducing patch rollout time or using other strategies to protect users while remediation is in progress. LLMs have also increased the volume of vulnerabilities that Project Zero reports. We are finding several vulnerabilities a week in targets where we once found a few vulnerabilities a year. Aspects of our policy that require vendor negotiation or agreement, including determining whether a bug is fixed and whether grace period applies, are quickly becoming unmanageable. Today, we are announcing a new vulnerability disclosure policy, created with the following goals in mind: Encourage faster vulnerability remediation Encourage vendors to reduce âpatch gapâ Allow for the policy to be automated by both Project Zero and vendors Our new policy: âFull Xâ Vulnerabilities will be disclosed X days after they are reported to the vendor. Starting today, our policy is âFull 90â, i.e. vulnerabilities will be disclosed 90 days after they are reported to the vendor. On February 2, 2027, we will move to a âFull 60â policy where vulnerabilities are disclosed after 60 days. On January 3, 2028, we will move to a âFull 30â policy where vulnerabilities are disclosed after 30 days. We are also removing most âspecial casesâ from our disclosure policy, including grace period and variant policy. The only exceptions to our new policy are: Vulnerabilities actively exploited in the wild -- ITW vulnerabilities will be handled according to Googleâs application security vulnerability disclosure policy Public vulnerabilities -- Project Zero may make details of a vulnerability public, at our discretion, if the details have already been made public by others Vendor request -- We will make vulnerability details public if the vendor we reported it to requests it Why reduce remediation time gradually? Project Zero solicited feedback from the vendors we report the most vulnerabilities to as a part of developing this new policy. An overarching concern was that immediately changing the policy could harm users by making unfixed vulnerabilities available to attackers while vendors are in the process of improving their remediation processes and technology. While the benefits of delaying disclosure are declining due to the increased probability that attackers will discover a vulnerability during the embargo period, we still feel there are benefits in the short term. In addition, vendors mentioned two more subtle concerns. One was that an overly-aggressive disclosure policy would encourage fixing bugs reported under the new policy with more priority, even if they are less severe than other reported vulnerabilities. The other was that immediately enforcing a policy that some vendors arenât equipped to meet might lead to a state where vendors accept that they cannot fix bugs within the deadline and donât attempt to. We decided on a policy that encourages vendors to improve remediation time on a schedule that is challenging but realistic, with the hope that this will lead to vendors broadly improving their remediation processes and infrastructure in a way that eventually enables them to fix all reported vulnerabilities quickly. What about severity? While our analysis isnât always perfect, Project Zero only reports vulnerabilities with substantial severity and demonstrated security impact in our tracker. That said, we donât feel severity is an effective metric for making disclosure decisions, especially in the current environment. A vulnerabilityâs severity does not affect the likelihood that it will be discovered by attackers, only its impact on users. When vendors determine severity and use it to prioritize bug fixes, they are making decisions about what risks they are willing to expose their users to, and it is reasonable to accept the risk of low-severity bugs, like unexploitable null pointer crashes or minor info leaks in a lot of circumstances. But this doesnât change the availability of these vulnerabilities to attackers, and we want our policy to reflect this reality. Itâs also important to acknowledge that Project Zero holds itself to high standards with regards to the reproducibility, readability, reachability and reported security impact of the vulnerabilities we report. This policy assumes bugs reports are of this quality, and it is reasonable for vendors to treat low quality-bug reports differently. What about hardware? We encourage all vendors to consider how they would respond to imminent disclosure of a serious vulnerability, including non-patch strategies , as there is no guarantee that defenders will be the first to find a bug. That said, Project Zero has occasionally granted exceptions to our policy on rare occasions, including Spectre and Meltdown, and will continue to do so in the future. Are you really not going to check whether bugs are fixed? The question of whether a bug is fixed for the purposes of our policy has always been challenging and somewhat unresolved, particularly with regards to code that is not shipped directly to users and not publicly available. It is not unusual for Project Zero to communicate with vendors multiple times for each bug report to come to an agreement on whether a vulnerability is fixed. As more vendors experiment with vulnerability remediation strategies that are not patching like temporarily disabling code paths, we expect this to become even more complex. We still plan to track whether bugs are fixed and communicate if they are not, however, this will not be a decision point in our policy. This will enable us to share technical details of how users are protected without needing to make a binary judgement with consequences for the vendor. Make zeroday hard. Privacy

title: PyPI's redesigned project pages with clearer security signals are now live
body_text: PyPI's redesigned project pages with clearer security signals are now live - The Python Package Index Blog Skip to content PyPI.org PyPI blog User documentation Developer documentation Navigation The Python Package Index Blog PyPI's redesigned project pages with clearer security signals are now live Search Search GitHub The Python Package Index Blog GitHub The PyPI Blog The PyPI Blog On this page Context The New Security Tab Provenance States Full Provenance No Provenance Provenance Warnings Incomplete Provenance Inconsistent Provenance Change of Provenance Loss of Provenance Redesigned Project Detail Page Release Files and Release History Getting Help Looking Ahead & Acknowledgments Archive Archive 2026 2025 2024 2023 Authors Authors Nicole Harris Jacob Coffee Maria Ashna Mike Fiedler William Woodruff Seth Larson Dustin Ingram Ee Durbin Facundo Tuesca Deb Nicholson Shamika Monahan Donald Stufft Tags On this page Context The New Security Tab Provenance States Full Provenance No Provenance Provenance Warnings Incomplete Provenance Inconsistent Provenance Change of Provenance Loss of Provenance Redesigned Project Detail Page Release Files and Release History Getting Help Looking Ahead & Acknowledgments Back to index Nicole Harris PyPI Design Contributor Metadata November 6, 2026 6 min read Related links Planned Updates to the PyPI User Interface PyPI now supports digital attestations Releases now reject new files after 14 days PyPI's redesigned project pages with clearer security signals are now live In July, we announced a series of planned updates to the PyPI user interface. Shaped by user research with members of the Python community , the updates aim to improve how we surface security signals and display package details. We're pleased to share that this work is now complete and live on PyPI . Context ¶ With the rapid growth of the Python ecosystem, PyPI has become an increasingly attractive target for malicious actors. In response, the PyPI team has delivered many security features while taking a more active role in helping PyPI users assess and understand package security. Digital attestations , introduced in 2024, are an example of this effort, providing a verifiable record of a release file's provenance (where it came from). However, provenance and attestations are still unfamiliar concepts for many PyPI users, and PyPI's interface did little to communicate their meaning, importance, or limitations. To address this, PyPI partnered with Kabu Creative to bring clearer security signals to the PyPI UI, implementing the recommendations developed in the OpenSSF Attestations Style Guide . Here's a look at what's changed, what it means for you, and what actions you can take. The New Security Tab ¶ The new security tab communicates release provenance states and displays per-file attestations, giving you a dedicated place to verify where the release files came from. The new security tab on a PyPI project detail page Provenance States ¶ PyPI calculates each release's provenance state by checking whether each release file has an attestation. Typically, a release will be in one of two states: Full Provenance ¶ This means that 100% of the release files have attestations, carrying either or both of the supported attestation types: PyPI Publish attestations confirm the file was published by a PyPI Trusted Publisher : An example PyPI Publish attestation on PyPI SLSA Build Provenance attestations link the file back to its exact source commit, build platform, and instructions: An example SLSA Build Provenance attestation on PyPI You can review attestation metadata directly in the UI, or click on the transparency log link for more information. No Provenance ¶ "No provenance" simply means that no file in the release has an attestation. This is typical for older releases or projects that have not yet configured Trusted Publishing. No provenance does not necessarily indicate that a release or release file is malicious; it instead means that the file origin cannot be cryptographically verified . When there is no provenance, you should rely on surrounding trust signals to assess security, such as maintainer history, release patterns, and repository activity. If you maintain the package, consider using Trusted Publishing with a publisher that generates attestations for your next release. Provenance Warnings ¶ Provenance warnings are designed to help you identify when a file may not have come from the project's maintainers, for example, if an attacker has taken over an account or a publishing workflow. When provenance metadata looks unusual or conflicts with a project's history, PyPI surfaces a prominent warning. Many warnings have legitimate explanations, but each one is worth checking before you install. Incomplete Provenance ¶ This means that some files carry attestations while others do not (e.g., wheels were published via Trusted Publishing, but the source tarball was uploaded using an API token). Exercise caution if you see this warning. Check release notes for build issues or ask in the project's issue tracker before installing. Inconsistent Provenance ¶ This warning indicates that files within the same release originate from different build systems or source repositories. Check the attestation metadata to confirm whether all files came from sources controlled by the maintainers. Change of Provenance ¶ This warning tells you that the release files originated from a different repository or workflow than a previous release. While often legitimate (such as an organization name change or repository migration), it can also indicate a compromised pipeline or account takeover. If you see this warning, check the project release notes or official channels to confirm that an infrastructure migration was planned. Loss of Provenance ¶ This means that a project that previously published with attestations has changed to uploading release files without them. Check whether the maintainers intentionally changed their publishing process, for example by switching back to API tokens, or by changing their publishing configuration so that it no longer generates attestations. If this is unexpected, treat the release with skepticism until verified. To learn more about provenance and attestations, including provenance warnings, see our user documentation . An example provenance warning on PyPI, showing a release with incomplete provenance Redesigned Project Detail Page ¶ To support these changes, the project detail page has also been updated: Provenance warnings now appear at the top of the page, alongside status banners for yanked releases, archived projects, and pre-releases. If a project or release is quarantined , only the quarantine banner is shown, as it takes precedence over all other warnings and banners. When a release has full provenance or provenance warnings, its provenance state is displayed in the sidebar, linking through to the security tab for more information. Metadata is now ordered by utility and labeled as "PyPI data" or "Data verified by PyPI", replacing the old design where data was grouped and ordered by verification status. The redesigned metadata sidebar, with information ordered by utility Release Files and Release History ¶ The redesigned release files tab helps you find the right file by searching and filtering long lists. You can also view the provenance state of each file within the table, and quickly identify late files, which are marked with an orange warning icon. Late file warnings are shown when one or more files were uploaded more than 14 days after the initial release timestamp. These warnings only appear on releases prior to July 2026, when a policy was introduced to reject new files after 14 days . The release history tab now also provides more details about each release, exposing file count, provenance state, and release status (i.e., quarantined, yanked, archived, or pre-release). The redesigned release history tab, with release status, file count, and provenance state Getting Help ¶ Alongside the interface updates, PyPI's user documentation has been extended to help you better navigate package security. Read our package security guide to learn about: Assessing source code security Checking provenance (where a package came from) Verifying package integrity Protecting yourself from common security attacks Reporting security issues Looking Ahead & Acknowledgments ¶ The new security tab gives PyPI a dedicated home for future attestation types and security notices. To help the wider open source ecosystem benefit from this work, we've also published a case study in the OpenSSF Attestations Style Guide detailing the design patterns and warnings developed during this project. This initiative was funded by the Open Source Security Foundation and implemented by Kabu Creative . We would like to thank Dustin Ingram , Zach Steindler , and the members of the OpenSSF Securing Software Repositories Working Group for championing this effort. Special thanks to Mike Fiedler , Jacob Coffee , and members of the PyPI team for their thoughtful design feedback and code reviews, @cofiem for their contributions to the new release files tab, and our user interview participants and community testers for helping shape the final design. Finally, we would like to thank the OpenSSF for its funding and continued partnership in securing the Python packaging ecosystem. security user-interface Back to top Previous Higher limits for organization projects Made with Zensical

title: Reverse engineering my Coway air purifier to ditch the cloud
body_text: Reverse Engineering My Coway Air Purifier to Ditch the Cloud | Scott's Blog Scott J. Goldman Posts RSS Reverse Engineering My Coway Air Purifier to Ditch the Cloud November 11, 2026 16 min read Nice enough air purifier, but I don’t love the app. The year is 2017. A string of annual wildfires rocks the West Coast. The sky looks like this in the daytime: My home, like many in the Bay Area, has no insulation and isn’t really air sealed. To avoid choking on soot, a lot of people started buying air purifiers like this one : The venerable Coway Airmega It’s an overpriced box fan with a HEPA filter and an air quality sensor. It has some controls for the fan speed, and it can also automatically ramp up if the air quality is bad. It’s ugly, but they’re so ubiquitous around here that I feel like no one even notices them anymore. Also, FWIW, the device works. It really does improve air quality. This device became a staple item in our household when my wife eventually started cranking up the fan at night for white noise (a dual purpose!). Over time, I have become accustomed to it and now also require it to sleep. The Good Night button # Our home also has smart lighting, and it’s all integrated with Apple Home. At night, I always press the “Good Night” button, which shuts off all the lights. I really wanted to tie the fan into that. I’d press Good Night, the lights would shut off, and the fan would crank up to my wife’s preferred white noise volume. The old Airmega didn’t have Wi-Fi, so there was no easy way to integrate it with Apple Home. When it eventually broke, I bought the now-discontinued Coway Airmega IconS (for non-discontinued Wi-Fi models, check out the Airmega 250S or Airmega MightyS ). It’s still just a box fan with a HEPA filter, but it’s considerably more expensive, aims to look like a piece of fancy mid-century furniture, and most importantly, can be controlled over Wi-Fi (sort of). The Coway Airmega IconS The existing Home Assistant integration # Coway’s iPhone app is an absolutely classic IoT affair. It takes forever to load, and it asks me to change my password nearly every time I launch it. Thankfully, a brave soul reverse-engineered the app and wrote an integration for Home Assistant . The integration more or less pretends to be the phone app. It polls the Coway cloud service for status updates and sends commands through it to control the fan. Home Assistant bridges that to Apple Home and… voilà! Coway IoCare cloud Coway's servers, somewhere on the internet commands ↑ status ↓ status ↑ commands ↓ My house Home Assistant IoCare integration Air purifier Airmega IconS, on Wi-Fi Apple Home the Good Night button Why ditch the cloud? # The downside of this approach is that you’re still at the mercy (or lack thereof) of the Coway cloud service. It seems like at least once or twice a year, it breaks. Here are some of the reasons I have seen it break: Coway didn’t like the integration hammering their servers and banned it. After a protracted argument with the community, they eventually settled on allowing it. Coway rewrote their phone app and rebranded it from IoCare to IoCare+, so the integration had to be rewritten as well. Coway made minor changes to the layout of the HTML that the integration scrapes, which broke it. Coway’s servers were periodically offline, which prevented any remote control of the device. Coway banned my account at one point for running an old version of the integration. I couldn’t control the fan remotely for weeks while I waited for their support team to reverse the ban. On top of this, it seems unlikely that Coway will maintain this service forever. I suspect that eventually, like all IoT manufacturers, they’ll either charge for this service or discontinue it. My fan model is already discontinued (though there are other Wi-Fi enabled models, so… who knows). A way in # I admit, I have been lazy. For years, I put off trying to figure out a way to ditch the Coway cloud, because if the device was really locked down, it would be pretty tough. Presumably, when the fan starts up, it connects to coway.com (or whatever) and checks that the server’s SSL certificate is valid. Most likely, I wouldn’t be able to make a fake certificate that passes that check, so the fan wouldn’t connect to my server. Also, setting up a man-in-the-middle (MitM) environment is just a pain in the neck. The fan would have to connect to an isolated Wi-Fi network that routes all its traffic through my own server on the way out to the internet. To do that, you have to configure a bunch of routing and firewall rules to redirect traffic. None of this is impossible (I’ve done it before), but it’s a hassle to set up, and it’s always finicky to get right. And once you have it set up, that’s just step one. All that said, two major things have changed. First, there was a recent security incident (October 2026) where someone discovered that eMudhra, one of the trusted internet certificate authorities, had used a very weak parameter for some of its private keys. Ian Carroll @iangcarroll For the next few days or weeks, anyone now has a root CA thanks to eMudhra. Time to have some fun with MiTMing unwilling devices! 10:15 AM · Oct 20, 2026 So, if the device is unpatched AND it has hardcoded root certificates AND it doesn’t pin the cloud service’s certificate, then… maybe that’s a way in. Admittedly, that’s a lot of ifs, but assuming the device doesn’t have any major security mistakes in its design, this could be the foothold needed to take control of it. The second thing is simply AI. An LLM can set up everything you need for a MitM environment, so you can get straight to sleuthing out how the fan works. It can do this unattended, in minutes. Once you can sit between the fan and the internet, you can see how it communicates, which should help us understand how to get the fan to talk to us instead of the cloud. Our man in the middle # Initially, I tried to set it up like this: Air purifier Airmega IconS Wi-Fi Raspberry Pi Wi-Fi access point the Pi in AP mode, its own isolated network all traffic redirected mitmproxy decrypts and logs the traffic My home router the regular home network Coway IoCare cloud out on the internet This actually didn’t work, because a Raspberry Pi uses a smallish PCB trace antenna that doesn’t get a ton of signal strength. With the Pi in the room with my router, the signal was too weak to reach the fan. I guess I could’ve moved the fan into the room with the router, but why do that when I can solve this with a convoluted technical solution? The Raspberry Pi uses its Wi-Fi radio to run its own access point for the fan to connect to. It can’t easily do that while also connecting over Wi-Fi to the home network. So, I moved the Pi into the room with the fan and plugged its Ethernet port into my laptop, which bridges it to the home network over Wi-Fi: Air purifier Airmega IconS Wi-Fi, same room Raspberry Pi Wi-Fi access point the Pi in AP mode, its own isolated network all traffic redirected mitmproxy decrypts and logs the traffic Ethernet My laptop Internet Sharing, bridging Wi-Fi to Ethernet Wi-Fi My home router the regular home network Coway IoCare cloud out on the internet Next, we need to configure the Pi. I’m not really making a value judgment here on whether this is a fair thing to block, but Claude will not oblige the request, not even for… uhh… testing purposes. Luckily, ChatGPT has no such compunctions. After a few rounds of that, here are the nftables rules it ended up with: scottjg@pi:~ $ sudo nft -a list ruleset table inet mitmproxy_ap { # handle 8 set client_interfaces { # handle 4 type ifname elements = { "wlan0" } } chain prerouting { # handle 1 type nat hook prerouting priority dstnat; policy accept; meta nfproto ipv4 iifname @client_interfaces tcp dport { 80, 443 } counter packets 2 bytes 120 redirect to :8080 # handle 6 } chain input { # handle 2 type filter hook input priority filter - 10; policy accept; iifname != "lo" iifname != @client_interfaces tcp dport 8080 counter packets 0 bytes 0 reject with tcp reset # handle 7 iifname @client_interfaces meta nfproto ipv6 counter packets 9 bytes 2397 drop # handle 8 iifname @client_interfaces ct state established,related accept # handle 9 iifname @client_interfaces udp dport { 53, 67 } accept # handle 11 iifname @client_interfaces tcp dport { 53, 8080 } accept # handle 13 iifname @client_interfaces ip protocol icmp accept # handle 14 iifname @client_interfaces counter packets 23 bytes 4697 reject with icmpx admin-prohibited # handle 15 } chain forward { # handle 3 type filter hook forward priority filter - 10; policy accept; iifname @client_interfaces meta nfproto ipv6 counter packets 0 bytes 0 drop # handle 16 oifname @client_interfaces meta nfproto ipv6 counter packets 0 bytes 0 drop # handle 17 iifname @client_interfaces udp dport 443 counter packets 1 bytes 57 reject # handle 18 iifname @client_interfaces oifname != "eth0" counter packets 0 bytes 0 reject with icmpx admin-prohibited # handle 19 } } table ip nm-shared-wlan0 { # handle 12 chain nat_postrouting { # handle 1 type nat hook postrouting priority srcnat; policy accept; ip saddr 10.42.0.0/24 ip daddr != 10.42.0.0/24 masquerade # handle 2 } chain filter_forward { # handle 3 type filter hook forward priority filter; policy accept; ip daddr 10.42.0.0/24 oifname "wlan0" ct state { established, related } accept # handle 5 ip saddr 10.42.0.0/24 iifname "wlan0" accept # handle 6 iifname "wlan0" oifname "wlan0" accept # handle 7 iifname "wlan0" reject # handle 8 oifname "wlan0" reject # handle 9 } } Basically, the masquerade rule translates the traffic from the isolated Wi-Fi network out through our home internet, and the redirect rule forwards HTTP/HTTPS to a running instance of mitmproxy . Also on the Pi, mitmproxy runs with its web interface, mitmweb , using a command line like this: mitmweb \ --mode transparent --showhost \ --listen-host 0.0.0.0 --listen-port 8080 \ --web-host 127.0.0.1 --web-port 8081 \ --set web_open_browser=false \ --emudhra-old Yes, off the shelf, mitmproxy has a built-in option ( --emudhra-old ) to automatically use the eMudhra root CA to intercept traffic. Snooping on the fan # Next, I used the iPhone app to set up the fan on our Pi-MITM-Test Wi-Fi network. Partway through, the app reported that setup failed. Let’s glance at the mitmproxy web interface: So, we know there was some kind of connection issue, since the app said the fan failed to connect. But it clearly got onto our isolated Wi-Fi, because it made a request . The request is very suspicious. It looks like the fan is downloading the root certificate for Amazon’s certificate authority over plain HTTP. This interface only shows connections that got far enough to make an actual HTTP request. If, for example, the fan doesn’t accept the eMudhra cert we’re using to impersonate the real servers, its HTTPS connections will fail before that point and never show up in the list. Hypothesis: The device downloads this public certificate over HTTP so it has something to validate its later (currently unseen) HTTPS connections against. It doesn’t have any root certificates built in at all. mitmproxy has a plugin mode where you can modify specific requests. We can use it to swap in mitmproxy ’s own generated CA certificate in place of this public one. If our hypothesis is correct, the fan will trust that CA, and we can intercept the rest of its traffic. """Serve this lab's public RSA CA only to the authorized Coway test device.""" from pathlib import Path from mitmproxy import ctx, http def response (flow: http . HTTPFlow) -> None : if ( flow . client_conn . peername[ 0 ] == "10.42.0.93" # device IP and flow . request . scheme == "http" and flow . request . method == "GET" and flow . request . pretty_host == "rootca-fs.iocareus.com.s3.ap-northeast-2.amazonaws.com" and flow . request . path . split( "?" , 1 )[ 0 ] == "/AmazonRootCA1.pem" and flow . response is not None and flow . response . status_code == 200 ): certificate = Path( "/var/lib/mitmproxy-ap/mitmproxy-ca-cert.pem" ) . read_bytes() flow . response = http . Response . make( 200 , certificate, { "Content-Type" : "application/x-pem-file" , "Cache-Control" : "no-store" , }, ) flow . metadata[ "coway_test_ca_served" ] = True ctx . log . info( "Served lab RSA CA to the Coway's HTTP CA bootstrap request" ) Sure enough, the device now fully connects, and we can see some new requests: Hypothesis confirmed We can intercept the traffic between the fan and the server, which means we could probably build our own server to replace the Coway IoCare cloud. It also turns out we don’t need the eMudhra hack at all. The fan downloads its root CA cert over plain HTTP. It was always MitM-able. The one thing missing is that none of these requests have anything to do with changing the fan speed or anything else you can do in the app. That’s easy to figure out, though. If you run tcpdump on the Pi while clicking buttons in the app, you can see encrypted traffic on port 8883, the standard port for MQTT over TLS. MQTT is a message bus protocol commonly used in IoT devices. Going back to the POST in the request list above, here’s what that API call returned: { "header": { "success": true, "result": "S1000", "message": "SUCCESS" }, "payload": { "macAddr": "<redacted>", "certToken": "<redacted>", "host": "a29vouc2qruduj-ats.iot.ap-northeast-2.amazonaws.com", "port": 8883, "serial": "<redacted>", "certSvrUrl": "https://cert.iotp.coway.com/iot/v1/cert/r0", "caUrl": "http://rootca-fs.iocareus.com.s3.ap-northeast-2.amazonaws.com/AmazonRootCA1.pem", "privateUrl": "https://icert-fs.iocareus.com/<redacted>/55d66923e9-private.pem.key", "certUrl": "https://icert-fs.iocareus.com/<redacted>/55d66923e9-certificate.pem.crt", "svcCode": "002AIR007", "countryCd": "US" } } So, if we control the response to this call, we control which keys the fan uses to connect to the MQTT server, and also where that MQTT server is. For now, we can write another mitmproxy plugin that injects our own key into this response, and then use that to proxy the MQTT traffic. The plugin code gets kinda long, so I didn’t include it here, but AI generates it fairly quickly. mitmproxy doesn’t decode MQTT, but it can still show us the raw stream: The data looks like a mix of binary and ASCII gibberish, but it’s a standard MQTT protocol stream. When I adjust the fan speed in the app, you can see a new message come from the Coway server to the device. Usually, I’d load this into a traffic dissector and make a table of what gibberish comes in when I press each button in the app, but now… and after a few minutes… There’s enough here now to build our own web server that hands the fan its certificates and configuration during setup, plus our own MQTT server to send it commands. That completely cuts the Coway cloud out of the picture during normal operation, but we’re still using the Coway app to set the device up. We also still need a fairly annoying MitM environment to get the fan to connect to us instead of Coway. Bluetooth setup process # When you use the Coway app to set up the fan, it searches for the device via Bluetooth. I was hoping we could figure out a way to configure the device ourselves, without the app. Plus, if we’re lucky, we might find something else useful along the way. I have reverse-engineered Bluetooth devices before . My old strategy was to get the Android version of the app, decompile it , and then just pore over the code. It’s not always as straightforward as it sounds. Developers often obfuscate their apps, which makes the decompiled code harder to read. Some bytecode also doesn’t decompile cleanly back to source code, which means you end up having to read the raw bytecode. Still, in my opinion, this is usually easier than dealing with iPhone apps. Android apps are usually written in Java (or Kotlin), and it’s just easier to reverse-engineer Java apps than apps compiled from Swift or Objective-C. This time, I tried a new strategy, which was to use the built-in Android Bluetooth debug logs. Then, I connected the phone over USB and asked the AI to drive the phone via adb , look at the Bluetooth logs, and reconstruct the protocol. The AI took a while to churn through this task. Eventually, it identified that the message carrying the Wi-Fi configuration was encrypted. Since we would ultimately need to figure out what algorithm was used for the encryption, we would probably have to look at the decompiled app. Sure enough, the next thing it did was pull the Coway app off the phone, decompile it. Then, it started matching up the source code with the Bluetooth logs. After all that, we can see the provisioning works like this: Read the fan’s identity over Bluetooth from characteristic FFA0 (a “characteristic” is a Bluetooth endpoint you can read or write). This gives you some basic information about the device, including its MAC address. Write an encryption key (20 random lowercase ASCII letters) to characteristic FFA2 : "P001" + protobuf { command: 1, key: Base64(random_letters) } Construct the AES key by concatenating the key from step 2 with the 12 uppercase ASCII characters of the MAC address. Build the configuration payload, which looks like this: { "cmd": 2, "ssid": "Example Wi-Fi", "pwd": "example-wifi-password", "bssid": "AABBCCDDEEFF", "type": 1, "macAddr": "112233445566", "caUrl": "http://192.0.2.1:8080/ca.pem", "certSvrUrl": "https://192.0.2.1:9443/iot/v1/cert/r0", "certToken": "example-enrollment-token", "serial": "EXAMPLE000000000001" } That gets wrapped in protobuf, padded with PKCS#7, and encrypted using the AES key from step 3. Then it gets prefixed with the string “P002” and sent to FFA2 as well. Needless to say, figuring this out end to end from the decompiled Android app would have been very time consuming to do by hand. It’d be at least hours of work (likely days). AI really comes in clutch here. It took the AI about 20 minutes. The good part, though, is that all the data you need to decrypt that payload is in the Bluetooth logs we captured from the phone, so we can check that our reimplementation is correct just from those. From there, the AI made quick work of reimplementing the whole setup flow in a little Python script. I was watching the progress pretty carefully while this was going on. The AI never actually showed me the full payload, but I could see it in the intermediate output of the scripts it was writing. And that’s when I noticed something. Two of the URLs from our capture are set right in this payload ( caUrl and certSvrUrl ). The first tells the fan where to download the root CA cert over plain HTTP, and the second tells it where to POST over HTTPS to get its MQTT configuration. Since we’re the ones sending this payload now, we can point those URLs anywhere we want. Most importantly, that means we don’t have to do any MitM anymore. We just have to run our own server and plug in its URLs when we set up the fan. Home Assistant integration # Based on the findings in this article, I was able to build a Home Assistant custom integration for the fan . My Home Assistant server doesn’t have Bluetooth, and it’s pretty far away from my fan, so I opted to do the provisioning with Web Bluetooth. That way you can bring your laptop next to the fan and provision it to talk to Home Assistant directly. After that, the device talks directly over Wi-Fi to Home Assistant. And, more importantly, it gets bridged from Home Assistant to my Apple Home. All in a day’s work. Now, I can finally click Good Night. If you liked this post, I can email you when I write another one. Subscribe I don't post that often, so it won't be much email. Just a quick FTC required note: When you buy through my links, I may earn a commission. Comments Comments are powered by Artalk and require JavaScript to load. You can also reach me on Mastodon . © 2026 Scott J. Goldman RSS

body_text: Apple has new Mac app coming to make running local AI models easy - 9to5Mac Skip to main content Toggle main menu 9to5Mac Logo Go to the 9to5Mac home page Switch site 9to5Toys 9to5Google Logo 9to5Google Electrek Drone DJ Logo DroneDJ Space Explored About Privacy Toggle social menu Toggle dark mode Search for: Submit Toggle search form Forums Store Podcasts Apple@Work Happy Hour 9to5Mac Daily Overtime iPhone iPhone Mac Mac MacBook Pro MacBook Air iMac Mac mini Mac Studio Mac Pro iPad iPad Pro iPad Air iPad mini iPad iPadOS Watch Apple Watch Apple Watch Ultra Apple Health Apple Watch SE Vision Vision Pro visionOS Music and TV Apple Music AirPods HomePod Apple TV Guides Reviews How Tos AAPL Apple Store Apple Arcade Apple Card Apple Silicon Apple One Apple Fitness+ CarPlay Siri HomeKit Toggle dark mode AI Apple has new Mac app coming to make running local AI models easy Ryan Christoffel  | Nov 10 2026 - 11:15 am PT 0 Comments Leaker Aaron Perris has discovered evidence of a new Mac app in the works at Apple called Harbor, which makes it easy to run local AI models across one or more Macs. New ‘Harbor’ app revealed at Apple: ‘turns your Mac into a private AI inference server’ The Mac has been getting a lot more popular this year, both because of budget-friendly options like MacBook Neo but also as a tool for running AI models locally on Mac Studio, Mac mini, and more. It seems Apple plans to lean harder into the latter use case, as leaker Aaron Perris has discovered a new Mac app called Harbor that’s been designed to turn your Mac into a private AI inference server. Here’s Perris’s post on X with the details: Apple is working on a new app called Harbor Harbor turns your Mac into a private AI inference server. Run open-weight models locally on Apple silicon—your data never leaves your hardware, and nothing reaches the cloud. Connect multiple Mac computers over Thunderbolt 5 to pool… pic.twitter.com/UYJBQeX4Nf — Aaron (@aaronp613) November 10, 2026 As the post notes, here’s what the app does: Harbor turns your Mac into a private AI inference server. Run open-weight models locally on Apple silicon—your data never leaves your hardware, and nothing reaches the cloud. Connect multiple Mac computers over Thunderbolt 5 to pool unified memory, enabling large models and higher concurrency that a single computer can handle alone. And here are the feature highlights: Setup in minutes, not hours : “Harbor automatically detects your devices over Thunderbolt 5 to form a cluster. Plug in, start, and you’re running—no manual configuration, no command line, no infrastructure expertise required.” Download and run models directly : “Browse, download, and load open-weight models from within the app. Harbor handles model management so you can focus on the work, not the setup.” Cluster for scale : “Connect two or more Thunderbolt 5-capable Mac computers and Harbor pools their unified memory into a single inference resource. Run models that exceed any single computer’s capacity, or serve more concurrent requests across your cluster.” Harbor is currently in a private preview under Apple’s Claris brand, but it seems likely that we’ll see it launch to the public in the weeks and months ahead. Are you interested in using Harbor on your Mac? Let us know in the comments. body_text: In Memoriam: Tim Peters 1952–2026 - Core Development - Discussions on Python.org = 40rem)" rel="stylesheet" data-target="discourse-ai_desktop" /> = 40rem)" rel="stylesheet" data-target="discourse-reactions_desktop" /> = 40rem)" rel="stylesheet" data-target="poll_desktop" /> Discussions on Python.org In Memoriam: Tim Peters 1952–2026 Core Development guido (Guido van Rossum) November 11, 2026, 5:36am 1 I am immensely sad to announce that Tim Peters has died earlier this year on July 15. It’s hard to overestimate Tim’s influence on Python. He’s probably best known for writing the Zen of Python ( PEP 20 ), but to me he was a mentor and language co-designer long before that. Tim found Python not long after its initial release. His first deed was to convince me that Python should support mixed arithmetic between int and float , because most users would expect them to work that way. And he never stopped contributing. Tim quickly became a major phenomenon on the Python mailing list (including later incarnations and spinoffs), where he earned the nickname “Timbot” by his innumerable, careful and patient answers to user questions. These he filled with mild humor (always marked by <wink> or <0.5 wink> ) and often referred to as “channeling Guido”. At the same time Tim participated in numerous in-depth design discussions, saving me or others from embarrassing design mistakes or solving deep problems, guided by his vast mathematical knowledge and compiler-building experience. In fact, Tim really set the tone for early core development, never outright dismissing people and explaining in detail why things could or couldn’t work. In 2002, Tim gave us Timsort : a new sorting algorithm he designed for Python lists, which was later adopted by Java and Android. Python-would-not-be-what-it-is-today-without-Tim-ly y’rs, –Guido 238 Likes guido (Guido van Rossum) November 11, 2026, 5:41am 2 Feel free to respond with your own Tim anecdotes. I could not cover everything he did. 12 Likes Rosuav (Chris Angelico) November 11, 2026, 6:04am 3 Very sad news. I have had the privilege and pleasure of discussing MANY topics with Tim, and his input into technical discussions has always been something I value very highly. He never treated you like an idiot, never dismissed your concerns out of hand, always answered and explained. I exchanged emails with him many times, but geography meant that sadly, we never met in person. 20 Likes hugovk (Hugo van Kemenade) November 11, 2026, 6:13am 4 Guido van Rossum: In fact, Tim really set the tone for early core development, never outright dismissing people and explaining in detail why things could or couldn’t work. From the start to the end. His last post concluded: Which is all a long-winded say of saying the real world is more complicated than our clean abstractions hope for . 51 Likes mcdonc (Chris McDonough) November 11, 2026, 6:41am 5 I wrote this some time ago about Tim: “”" I worked with Tim and the rest of Python Labs for a couple of years in the early 2000s. Tim was a hugely positive influence on me throughout my Python career. Before I had ever spoken to Tim, he was already legendary. He had worked for Cray Research writing compilers for supercomputers, and for Dragon Systems, writing speech-to-text software at a time when such a task was considered largely impossible. He took up Python on a lark in its very early days, becoming something like Python’s second real user after Guido. Guido came to rely on Tim heavily. Tim will demur about this, but as far as I can tell, Tim and Guido were largely partners in the design evolution of very early Python, and before most important features made it in to Python, you could be sure that they had been examined from every angle, shaken, stirred, and thunk about very hard by both of them. Tim often played the role of gatekeeper and polisher. You have Tim to thank at least partially if you were a refugee from Java or Microsoft languages, which made excuses for their sprawling verbosity, complexity, and poor readability. Python, at the time, made none of those and had none of that (it now does). Tim was crucial in ensuring it stayed that way during his most active years. He will claim differently, but, by my observation, it is no accident that Python ballooned in complexity after his exit as day-to-day core developer. Perhaps this was more due to the resignation of Guido as BDFL and the new Steering Council model, which was also coincident, but not having Tim around didn’t help either. It was pure joy to read Tim’s Usenet and mail list posts, which were full of humor and good nature and measured positivity and not a little winking darkness. They somehow resonated with me on my journey from becoming a new programmer to a not-so-new programmer and they lit a path to becoming one on which you could be dramatically competent without becoming cryptic and insufferable. He was intensely knowledgeable, and unfailingly precise when arguing for or against some design change. But he was always gentle and patient and matter-of-fact, preferring to use humor and warmth rather than bile and authority as the currency in which he dealt. Tim penned “the Zen of Python” (“beautiful is better than ugly…”) which can be seen via “import this” to this day. You can see a bit of his wonderful humor and style in the prelude to his introduction of the poem . His enthusiasm was infectious, and in the days when he was most involved, most everyone could be witnessed spouting Tim-isms (winks and “'lys” and whatnot). When I did get the chance to work with Tim, he was just as influential. He had absolutely no pretensions. If I hadn’t already known him to be a computer savant, I would have assumed he was a biker or mechanic due to his long grey locks, full mustache and and working-class fashion sense. I would later find out that he had indeed worked at Harley-Davidson. I think he’s originally from Wisconsin, but an East- or West-Coaster not fluent in Midwest tongues could be excused for believing his disarming accent is Chicagoan. He seemed just like a regular-looking neighborhood punch-the-clock guy, not unlike all the mechanics and deliverymen and cooks and dishwashers and event staff I’d worked around as a kid and in my 20s. Except he was pretty much the smartest guy in every room he entered. Tim’s demeanor and lack of pretense inspired me to think that despite my own lack of education and pedigree, with enough effort and grace, that I might become a half-competent programmer. And eventualy I did. But before meeting Tim, it was not a given. I was alienated by the pretensions of my community peers, and I was often reminded that they were not necessary only by Tim. He was somewhat private. He could often be found with a pen and paper outside the building just standing alone, staring blankly off into space, presumably thinking about some mind-boggling algorithmic topic with which he had just been charged by our CTO, or perhaps mentally designing some aspect of a pet project, scribbling something every few minutes. He applied himself to our code, which included a custom database written in C and Python. He diagnosed and fixed a data-destroying bug in that byzantine codebase for our largest customer. This saved the account, and likely gave us enough runway for another year or so. Everyone who worked there was in awe of his programming and debugging skills, and while we tried our best to let the poor man be, we often asked him questions, many of which were pedestrian and dull. I remember one of our teammates trying to engage him into a debugging session, claiming that some fault seemed to happen every six runs. He smiled winkingly and asked “have you grepped the source for six?” It was a minor jab but given the sincerity of the question, and the person from which it had come, it occurred to me at the time that it might not be the worst theory of debugging from which to start. Tim was a Director of the Python Software Foundation from 2001 to 2014, bringing Python across an uncanny valley from a time where it was “interesting but ignorable” to “the planet’s default language” along with a cast of other incredible people. If you use Python, it’s not in small part due to Tim. When I started my own open source projects, it was Tim whom I channeled during design discussions and sprints. I quite consciously used tricks I had learned from him to make the process fun and welcoming. Rather than become prickly about some technical conflict, I would try to use low-brow humor to defuse things and I would try very hard to learn everything I could about the topic before responding such that I could gain and rely on the respect of other contributors. I often failed, of course, because I’m not Tim, but I was at least a twentieth a Tim, and at the time, I think my co-contributors would have agreed that the projects I led were fun and worthwhile to work on. It is in this way that Tim’s influence is likely most obvious to people today, because I’m not the only one who channeled him; any Python project started between 1995 and 2010 has a bit of Tim culture in it. “”" In sadness, . C 44 Likes duncathan (Dunc Graham) November 11, 2026, 6:46am 6 As a young child, only about 15, I first learned timsort. Some dozen years later, I had the briefest opportunity to exchange words with Tim himself on this forum. What a treat to have had that chance, just in time. RIP 12 Likes encukou (Petr Viktorin) November 11, 2026, 8:32am 7 When I was finishing university, head full of textbook algorithms, I read Objects/listsort.txt and was overwhelmed by how much depth, rigor, common sense and humanity can fit in a technical note. That was when I picked a programming language. 34 Likes pitrou (Antoine Pitrou) November 11, 2026, 9:53am 8 Tim’s main legacy for me has been the Zen of Python, which - despite being less cited nowadays - has been so useful and influential as a framework for elegance and clarity, and has informed so many people in their daily practice (and I cannot find a better way to describe him than as an excellent practitioner ). He was already less active when I started contributing around 2007; in fact my most frequent interactions with him have been in the recent years while he grew a slightly more confrontational attitude in some discussions, including here on d.p.o. I believe [1] he was acting with the best of intentions and was still deeply caring for the community he had been such a pivotal member of; acting with the same objectives as others, but having trouble to understand that different means might be used towards the same ends. and I might be full of myself here ↩︎ 20 Likes malemburg (Marc-André Lemburg) November 11, 2026, 9:58am 9 This is so sad and such a big loss for Python. Tim has given us a lot and we owe him. He was one of the extremely smart people who drew me into PythonLand in the late 1990s. Coming out of university, I was amazed how approachable, down to earth and humurous really great folks can be. Rest in Peace, Tim, and thanks-for-being-one-of-those-great-people-ly, Marc 22 Likes pf_moore (Paul Moore) November 11, 2026, 10:51am 10 So sad. I never had the chance to meet Tim in person, but his posts were always a delight to read, full of knowledge, insight and humour. I learned more than I can express from him. He will be missed. 16 Likes hodgestar (Simon Cross) November 11, 2026, 10:55am 11 One of the great souls, and roughly treated here near the end. 15 Likes nas (Neil Schemenauer) November 11, 2026, 12:31pm 12 A +1 to what Chris wrote. Tim was always pragmatic, preferring simple solutions over complex ones. In the early days of syntax highlighting in text editors, like Emacs and Vim, I remember that Python’s triple-quoted strings were tricky to get right. They span multiple lines and opening and closing tokens are identical, so it’s easy to get out of sync. Doctests make things especially tricky. I was telling Tim about some techniques I was using in the Vim syntax file to make it work more reliably. I don’t recall the editor Tim used (some commercial program on Windows) but he explained how he did it in his editor. Open the syntax highlighting config window, for open string token, type three quotes, for close string, type three quotes, close config window. Job done. That tickled him. He primarily used Windows 95 or 98 at a time when many Python core devs used NT, Unix, or Linux. He said if you installed all of Microsoft’s updates, it was quite reliable. Maybe he preferred it because it worked for him and there was no reason to change. Or, he found it useful when supporting people, since Windows was the most common platform Python was used on. Tim was about the furthest thing from an elitist you could be. This Bible quote comes to mind for me: “Ye shall know them by their fruits.”. Tim gave us a lot of fruit. I poked around at Python 2.4, since that seems a good version to show off the things he worked on. His contributions were all over the codebase but I’ll point out a few that stand out to me. pymalloc was contributed by Vladimir Marangozov but it was Tim who polished it to diamond-like form. A memory allocator is one of those things where it is impossible to have something completely optimal; you always make tradeoffs. Tim’s special contribution in that unit is Py_ADDRESS_IN_RANGE . It is well commented, if you want to understand how it works. Technically, it relies on undefined behavior but Tim figured it should work in practice. It did so for many years. At some point I wanted to increase the pymalloc pool size, since typical RAM sizes had increased so much since 2000. Tim helped me optimize the address_in_range() check. TimSort is a good example of Tim’s approach to software problems. Someone must have “nerd sniped” him on the problem of sorting. He already had an encyclopedic knowledge of the classic algorithms, like you’d find in Knuth. He spent a few days reading the recent research papers on sorting. With that knowledge and throwing in a few twists of his own, he made TimSort. He was always thinking of the common case, the favorable case as well as the worst-case scenarios. TimSort does all three well (it exploits already sorted runs, and uses galloping during merging to copy long stretches efficiently). Speaking of Knuth, the dict object algorithms were heavily optimized by Tim. The C file contains lots of comments. He also wrote dictnotes , which is a good example of his technical writing. Another example is weakref.txt , which I think Tim wrote after fixing a particularly difficult GC bug revealed by ZODB (while working at Zope Corp). On the topic of GC, the initial version of the cyclic garbage collector was written by me, merged before the 2.0 release. It was Tim who polished it into robust and well-performing shape. Likewise, I wrote the initial version of “simple generators” but it was Tim who put them on solid foundation, both the PEP and the implementation. Tim was skilled with numerical algorithms and error analysis, and Python benefited from his expertise. The float object and math module got special attention from him. He also worked on the Karatsuba multiplication algorithms in longobject . In addition to the C code, Tim also wrote beautiful Python code. As an example, see the N-Queens and Knight’s tour solvers in test_generators.py . He wrote the initial version of doctest . Some more examples of his work: difflib , pickletools , tabnanny (she shows no mercy!). It’s clear that Tim enjoyed writing code and solving problems. It’s also the case that he spent many thousands of hours of his time doing things primarily to help his fellow humans, without expectation of financial gain or of glory. Thank you, friend, for that and thank you for setting such an example. Edit: oops, my memory failed in terms of dictnotes, that was Raymond Hettinger’s work. I was thinking of listsort.txt . 47 Likes vinitkme (Vinit Kumar) November 11, 2026, 12:58pm 13 Thanks for everything Tim. Zen of Python has always been and will be my programming " North Star" and I strive to use it in every language I work with. Your impact has been on many of us Python Programmers and our families lives. Thank you and rest in peace! 10 Likes Stefan2 (Stefan Pochmann) November 11, 2026, 1:09pm 14 I’ve been fearing this since I noticed his absence end of July, dreading the thought whenever I saw his name but still no new activity. I’ve had quite a few interactions with Tim, he was one of my main contact points to Python, and he was the one who added me to Misc/ACKS . Thank you for everything, Tim. 8 Likes Paddy3118 (Paddy3118) November 11, 2026, 1:30pm 16 GNU Tim. 5 Likes diegor (Diego Russo) November 11, 2026, 2:39pm 17 I wish I’d had the chance to meet Tim in person. We had just a few exchanges on social media, but I always enjoyed reading his messages. There was always something to learn from his experience, his perspective and his way of thinking. Reading the memories shared here by those who knew and worked with him makes me regret even more that I never had that opportunity. I remember when Timsort was created. I was at university, studying algorithms, and it was a big deal at the time. But it’s the Zen of Python that influenced me most personally. “Now is better than never.” That sentence has stayed with me since I started using Python in the early 2000s. Over the years, it has become one of my personal mottos, encouraging me to keep trying, strive to do better and step outside my comfort zone, both in life and at work. We’ll probably never know what the 20th aphorism of the Zen of Python would have been. But perhaps that’s OK. I like to think that Tim left us the freedom to fill that space with something meaningful to each of us. Thank you, Tim, for everything you gave to Python and for the impact your work and words had on people. Rest in peace. 16 Likes holdenweb (Steve Holden) November 11, 2026, 3:09pm 18 Tim and I originally thought we first met fairly shortly after we both moved to Virginia, and became friends over Chinese lunches and discussions with Guido about starting a new Python conference. As we got to know each other better we realised that we had seen each other once before, when I visited a fellow academic’s office in Manchester, England, and Tim was there representing Cray Research back in 1983. Small world. After PythonLabs dissolved on Guido’s departure for the West coast the lunches eventually became a regular date at our local PF Chang, where Tim would invariably end with their huge “Mountain of Chocolate” dessert. The resulting sugar rush was often amusing. Tim was well-known long before I arrived in the Python world, and remained so after I left it. His technical contributions to Python, now the most popular programming language in the world, are legion. Just as significant, if not more so, was the way he communicated the joy, both of being a programmer and a human being. He was deeply affected by the ban imposed on him for ideological reasons by the Python Steering Committee but did not let that affect his desire to help others, which was on display until the end. I respected Tim above anyone else in the Python world for his wisdom, his witty humour and his deep humanity. There won’t be another one like him. Goodbye, old friend. 28 Likes sdeibel (Stephan Deibel) November 11, 2026, 3:41pm 19 This is very sad. I worked with Tim for quite a few years in context of the PSF board and of course also knew him from IPC and PyCons, starting in the relatively early days. He stood out to me almost immediately because so obviously utterly brilliant and yet with such a kind, helpful, respectful, good-humored way about him. One of the best people I’ve known, he was an inspiration to me and I think clearly also to very many others. Thanks, Tim, you will be missed. 13 Likes mwichmann (Mats Wichmann) November 11, 2026, 3:42pm 20 I only met Tim once, along with Guido, in 2001. I was writing a Python training course, and the training company wanted to arrange for “the experts” to get a look at it, so on a week I was in Reston working on it, we sat down over a meal. It wasn’t a very good course (“if I knew then what I know now”, a quarter century later…), but they generously gave of their time to critique, including Tim’s trademark humor, and I so appreciated it. He will be missed! 8 Likes mdickinson (Mark Dickinson) November 11, 2026, 4:00pm 22 Tim was hugely influential on my own CPython core development journey. Initially that influence was through his voluminous writings, mailing list discussions and his code itself: when I joined the core dev team in 2008, Tim himself was absent from the scene in person, but very much present through his many many contributions. Later on, after his return to core development, I was privileged to interact more directly with Tim on many topics. His gentle erudition, his humour and his patience were endless. Rest in peace, Tim. You will be sorely missed. 18 Likes next page → Home Categories Guidelines Terms of Service Privacy Policy Powered by Discourse , best viewed with JavaScript enabled

title: Rust 1.100
body_text: Announcing Rust 1.100.0 | Rust Blog Rust Blog Rust Install Learn Tools Governance Community 🖌 Light Dark System Announcing Rust 1.100.0 Nov. 12, 2026 · The Rust Release Team The Rust team is happy to announce a new version of Rust, 1.100.0. Rust is a programming language empowering everyone to build reliable and efficient software. If you have a previous version of Rust installed via rustup , you can get 1.100.0 with: $ rustup update stable If you don't have it already, you can get rustup from the appropriate page on our website, and check out the detailed release notes for 1.100.0 . If you'd like to help us out by testing future releases, you might consider updating locally to use the beta channel ( rustup default beta ) or the nightly channel ( rustup default nightly ). Please report any bugs you might come across! What's in 1.100.0 stable Never type Allocator API DropGuard API Conjuring zero-sized types Reporting unused dependencies in Cargo Reducing Cargo cache collisions Cargo min-publish-age Stabilized APIs Never type After 10 years and 5 failed stabilization attempts, the never type is finally stable ! This also completes the project goal for this work. The never type, spelled ! in code, is the canonical uninhabited type. It represents the type of diverging computations – computations which never resolve to any value – where any code that follows is unreachable. Expressions that terminate control flow, such as return , break , and std::process::exit , also have the type ! . Since having a value of the never type is impossible, Rust permits a never-to-any coercion, allowing to turn ! into any other type (this is what distinguishes it from any other uninhabited types). This can be used, for example, to not return a value from one of the branches of a match or an if : fn mrrrow ( option : Option < u32 > ) { let value = match option { // `x` has type `u32` Some ( x ) => x , // `return` has type `!`, which is then coerced to `u32`, // allowing the `match` to pass type checking. None => return , } ; // ... } While the never type could already be used and observed this way, and even named in the return type of functions ( -> ! ), this release allows naming the never type anywhere: fn infallible_unwrap < T > ( res : Result < T , ! > ) -> T { // ^^ writing `Result<_, !>` was not allowed before let Ok ( v ) = res ; v } Additionally this release changes Infallible to be an alias to the never type. That makes all old APIs that used Infallible be compatible with using ! . This was the plan ever since the introduction of Infallible and is one of the reasons why the never type stabilization was so hard (waffle gave a talk about some of the troubles of the stabilization). Unfortunately, to allow changing Infallible , we had to introduce a breaking change. This release changes the "never type fallback" from () to ! in editions before 2024 (i.e. 2015, 2018, and 2021), similarly to what has already been done in edition 2024 . This should largely be unnoticeable, but can affect code in some rare cases (for example when ignoring a result of a function returning a generic parameter). Note that this change might also make the compiler detect more code as unreachable. We tried to minimize the impact of this breaking change as much as possible, by providing future compatibility warnings far in advance and releasing fixes to public crates that have been broken by this. If a dependency is failing due to issues with the never type, consider updating it, as a fix might have already been released for it. Allocator API This release brings about the stabilization of the core parts of allocator_api , enabling library authors to define custom allocators that can be used together with certain standard library types - currently Vec and Box . These are enabled through the newly-stabilized Allocator trait. This is the foundation of the Allocators 1.0 project goal . A lot remains to be done still, including expanding the API surface usable with custom allocators and stabilizing their use on more collections and pointer types; with the core trait and design out of the way though, expect to see more being stabilized soon! DropGuard : run a closure on every exit path The Drop trait in Rust makes it possible to run code when a variable goes out of scope, regardless of whether we return , ? , or panic. Drop being a part of types means that in Rust you never have to close a socket . Implementing Drop can however feel a little inconvenient when all you want is to run some code unconditionally when a function exits. This is why we’re introducing core::mem::DropGuard : a new helper type that runs a closure when dropped. DropGuard takes two arguments: a variable and a closure. It implements Deref and DerefMut so you can keep working with the variable as normal. But when dropped it runs the closure and consumes the variable. DropGuard also implements a dismiss associated function [1] which returns the variable from the guard without running the destructor. This makes it possible to quickly implement all-or-nothing transaction-like APIs with a rollback. Here is an example implementing a parser which uses a guard to roll back mutations in case of failure: use std :: mem :: DropGuard ; use std :: num :: ParseIntError ; /// Attempt to parse all `strings` and push them into `nums`. /// If parsing any of them fails, `nums` remains unchanged. fn parse_all ( nums : & mut Vec < u32 > , strings : & [ & str ] ) -> Result < ( ) , ParseIntError > { let len = nums . len ( ) ; let mut nums = DropGuard :: new ( nums , move | nums | { nums . truncate ( len ) ; // ← 1. Reset the vec on failure } ) ; for s in strings { nums . push ( s . parse ( ) ? ) ; // ← 2. If `?` returns an error, roll back } DropGuard :: dismiss ( nums ) ; // ← 3. Parsing successful, dismiss the guard Ok ( ( ) ) } Conjuring zero-sized types As Rust's unsafe code guidelines are still being decided, it became clear that it would be very useful to decide what exactly it means to create zero-sized types in an unsafe way, and what we should recommend for people to do this. This question is answered in Rust 1.100 with a single function: std::mem::conjure_zst . Instead of transmuting () , MaybeUninit::uninit().assume_init() , or various other incantations, this is the dedicated way to create a value of a zero-sized type when you know that doing so is safe to do. If an inhabited type has no size, we know exactly what value it must be: nothing. Of course, APIs often rely on the inability to construct such types for safety, and that's why this function is unsafe. For example, PyO3's Python<'py> is a zero-sized marker token that represents holding the Python GIL (global interpreter lock). Many of Python's APIs require holding this lock to be safe, but conjuring a token from thin air would allow safe PyO3 calls to violate that precondition. Reporting unused dependencies in Cargo Building dependencies that are no longer used or are only needed for specific platforms can slow down builds. Rustc has the unused_crate_dependencies lint for this but it has false positives when used with Cargo because dependencies may be shared between multiple build targets, e.g. dependencies.tracing-subscriber being available for every bin in a package when only some may use it. Cargo now reports unused dependencies to users, e.g. warning: unused dependency `tracing-subscriber` --> Cargo.toml:23:1 | 23 | tracing-subscriber.workspace = true | ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^ | = note: `cargo::unused_dependencies` is set to `warn` by default help: consider removing the dependency on `tracing-subscriber` A limitation of this warning is that it will only appear when building every build target that may use an entry in a dependencies table. For example, running cargo check --bin foo won't show warnings for unused [dependencies] because another bin may be present that uses them. No warning will be shown for unused dev-dependencies because there isn't a way to ensure every development build target is built. This warning is being introduced as part of a new linting system for Cargo, controlled by the [lints.cargo] table in Cargo.toml , completing this project goal . See also the other lints that have been introduced . Reducing Cargo cache collisions Cargo builds all libraries and binaries in the build-dir and then uplifts final artifacts to the target-dir . At this time, these share a common parent directory. Different build configurations, like --features , can lead to different copies of libraries and binaries in the build-dir . These copies are kept unique by a build-configuration hash but this hash was not always applied due to platform constraints. This can lead to extra rebuilds, missed rebuilds, confusion over what binaries or libraries are used, and so on. These problems get exacerbated when sharing a build-dir across git worktrees. The build-dir now consistently applies the build-configuration hash to all content by organizing the directories around their build step, rather than their file type, and moving the hash from a file's name to the parent directory. This work began with the build directory layout project goal in 2025, and its stabilization is a milestone toward a new project goal , unblocking future improvements such as cache garbage collection, cross-workspace cache de-duplication, cross-workspace caching, and fine grain locking. We previously published a call for testing for the changes that are now taking effect. While this is an internal change, this may break build processes and tests that had workarounds for missing or incomplete features. In some cases, the workaround is no longer needed. See cargo#17287 for possible solutions and to add any new use cases. Cargo min-publish-age a.k.a. dependency cooldowns Malicious versions of packages are often caught within hours or days after being published, by either automated scanners or by the community. Rust 1.100 stabilizes Cargo's min-publish-age aware dependency resolution, which lets you wait for that window before it picks up newly published versions. This practice is also known as dependency cooldowns. You can opt in via .cargo/config.toml : [ registry ] global-min-publish-age = " 3 days " When selecting versions, Cargo now skips any version published more recently than that, and tells you what it held back: $ cargo update Updating crates.io index Locking 2 packages to highest compatible version as of min-publish-age Adding cc v1.11.0 (available: v1.18.0, published 3 hours ago) Adding clap 4.6.7 (available: 4.6.9, published 2 days ago) When a new version is needed right away, you can override the check for a single update: $ CARGO_RESOLVER_INCOMPATIBLE_PUBLISH_AGE = a l l o w cargo update clap - -precise 4.6.9 Updating crates.io index Updating clap 4.6.7 -> clap 4.6.9 (published 2 days ago, minimum age 3 days) The newer version will be recorded in Cargo.lock and kept from then on until a later cargo update re-resolves it. A few things to keep in mind: This depends on the registry recording when each version was published. Versions without a pubtime field in the index are never held back. cargo install ignores the minimum publish age, for both the installed crate and its dependencies. Pin a version with cargo install foo@1.2.3 if needed. Cooldowns reduce the risk from some supply chain attacks but are not a complete defense on their own. Please keep reviewing dependency updates as you otherwise would. Further work to protect the ecosystem is planned under the crates.io supply chain hardening project goal , including quarantine support and automated detection of suspicious releases.
